title: Cartier Cristallor Ref. 78096 - White Enamel 'Paris' Dial
description: Cartier's catalog is full of pieces that don't bear "Tank" in front of the model name, and many remain overlooked or flat out unknown to the vast majority of consumers. Introduced in 1973 as a part of the Louis Cartier Collection, the Cristallor is a textbook example of one such model. Produced in a handful of variants over the years, in a number of different metals, sizes, and with different movements, this is another gorgeous execution of Cartiers ubiquitous design language. The piece that we have here is an early example from circa the early 1970s. The solid yellow gold case comes in at 28mm x 34mm and features a hexagonal 'stepped' design with 'hidden' lugs, a sapphire cabochon crown, and a manual-winding movement within. The dial inside is exactly what you'd expect to find from Cartier during this era, with a white enamel surface, printed black 'Roman' indices with an inner chemin de fer minute track. Of course, everything is tied together with a blued-steel 'sword' handset. If nothing from the Tank or Santos family speaks to you, this might just be a perfect alternative, and quite a bit more rare.

title: Rolex Explorer II Ref. 16570 - Cream 'Rail' Dial R-Serial
description: The Rolex Explorer’s core has always been in rugged expedition. While it was originally born out of the Everest celebratory Explorer I - the Explorer II was designed for cave diving. Officially known as spelunking ! While the initial run of Explorer II, the Reference 1655, or 'McQueen' ( spoiler: there is no evidence of a connection or that he ever wore one, but the nickname stuck! ) had black dials with orange accents, while later iterations like the Ref. 16570 added a white dial to the mix. These are commonly referred to as ‘Polar’ dials and they are among the most striking Rolex dials of the last 40 years or so, due to their monochromatic scheme with gloss white dials and blackened outer white gold indices. The watch that we have here, however, is something slightly different to your typical 'Polar.' Following the release of the first 'Polar,' the Ref. 16550, was the Ref. 16570. The earliest examples look virtually identical to their predecessor, while slightly later variants have a few small differences that present themselves, most notably in the form of the dial. B ecause of the way white dials in this era were produced, a small run of these early pieces have aged over the years to a variety of cream-tones and were ultimately 'fixed' and phased out. The example that we have here, is one of those early watches, dating to circa 1988. It is amongst the earliest of the Ref. 16570, featuring the revised steel 24-hr bezel and updated movement. The Oyster case retains prominent and correct finishing throughout and shows normal wear, with light wear present on the bezel and minimal loss of black paint. The Oyster bracelet also shows matching wear and remains unpolished with only faint 'stretch.' The real highlight here, however, is that dial. It has aged to a desirable cream tone and rather than the black-painted white gold indices, it carries over both the 'white gold surrounds' and handset, devoid of the black paint, and the 'rail' text on the lower half of the dial. This is a highly elusive variant of the Explorer II by any standards, likely only in production for 6-12 months before this dial was phased out in favor of the black painted white gold indices and handset. All things considered, this is an excellent and compelling example of a neo-vintage model with a cult following, and frankly, are surfacing less and less on the open market.

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Triple Calendar Ref. 2721 - 'Brushed' Salmon Dial Unpolished
description: Jaeger-LeCoultre is one of the most well-rounded and storied brands in the history of watchmaking. They are not only known for models, but also, at least in the world vintage watches, equally known for their movements — a surprisingly unique accolade that is perhaps unmatched by any other brand. Be there no doubt, the most popular and well-known model from the brand is the properly iconic Reverso, but the brand offers so much more with model families like the Memovox, the Deep-Sea, and a wide range of complicated calendar timepieces. The piece that we have here is one of the latter, a 'triple calendar' dating to circa the late 1940s. The stainless steel case is wonderfully sized at 36mm in diameter with gorgeous 'banded' profiles, equally gorgeous 'teardrop' lugs, and a 'flat' crown and micro-pushers on the right profile. This is 1940s JLC at its best! Inside, the dial seems to further elevate the fantastic case. Salmon in color, it features a 'brushed' surface with applied rose gold-tone 'stud' and 'dart' indices, an oversized, 'concentric' running seconds register, and a contrasting white ring with printed red date numerals. The calendar apertures also work some red into the mix in the form of red printed day and month disc, and the rose gold-tone 'dauphine' handset with red-tipped calendar hand ties everything together beautifully. This piece is powered by JLC's manual-winding Calibre 464 and comes fitted to one of our 'granite' leather straps which, we think, allows that dial to pop properly. In many ways, this piece has a ton to offer. Outstanding overall condition, historically interesting, and uniquely styled... ...and for the price of a steel Datejust, hard to beat!

title: Breitling Premier Ref. 777 'Jumbo' - 'Brushed' Pink Dial
description: Breitling has a long and rich history in chronographs — with an emphasis on aviation chronographs. And like so many other brands who have a watch model, or family that has become synonymous with the brand name itself, the Navitimer is just that for Breitling. As a result, the Navitimer casts a substantial shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the SuperOcean, Top Time, and lesser-known pieces that pre-date model ranges all together. The example that we have here is one of the latter: A chronograph from the Premier family dating to circa 1945. Offered in phenomenal overall condition, this piece possesses many of the hallmark design characteristics found in both vintage Breitling chronographs as well as a handful of other stunning chronographs from this era. The case is crafted out of rose gold and measures in at 37mm in diameter, with attractive, downward curving lugs, 'pump' pushers, a screw-down caseback, and a 'stepped' bezel. It shows normal signs of wear with nice, defined finishing present throughout and a wild, purple oxidation on the right case profile around the crown and pushers. The dial is simply gorgeous. Wonderfully preserved, the 'salmon'-tone surface features a gently 'brushed' finishing along with excellent printed scales, 'concentric' subsidiary registers, and absolutely stunning rose gold 'foil' numerals at both 12 & 6 o'clock. Everything is tied together with a blued-steel handset, which exhibits an almost purple tarnishing that also matches that right case profile nicely. It is powered by a manual-winding Calibre 175 from Venus. Design details like the elegant and perfectly-sized case, the two-register dial layout with those 'foil' indices, and the pink-on-pink construction is an elusive and sought-after combination not often seen in any decade. Examples in condition like this simply do not surface on the open market all that often, and theres no saying if or when this configuration will again.

title: Auricoste Spirotechnique Ref. 906.21.05 'M.N.' - Matte Black Tritium Dial W/ Decommission Papers
description: Auricoste was established in France as a manufacturer supplying timepieces to the French Military and Navy, with civilian models produced as a secondary line. As a result, the overwhelming majority of surviving Auricoste watches trace their origins to military contracts. La Spirotechnique, founded in 1947 by Jacques Cousteau and Emile Gagnan, began as the distributor for Cousteau's newly developed Aqua-Lung regulator, and the company built its reputation supplying professional-grade diving equipment to divers worldwide. Beyond civilian markets, Spirotechnique became a key supplier of diving gear, watches included, to the French Navy and Army. Its American operations were established under the name U.S. Divers Company, an entity later rebranded as Aqua Lung. The brand crossover doesn't stop there, however. The piece that we have here utilizes a case design originally utilized by Heuer in their Deep Dive model, but production for Auricoste was contracted out to Zodiac. So, what we've got here is one heck of a compilation of brand stories all rolled into one piece that just happens to have been issued to the French Navy; better known as the Marine Nationale. Dating to the early 1990s, the case is 41.5mm in diameter and is made from stainless steel, with both a screw-down caseback and crown. Thanks to the 4 o'clock position of the crown and being largely recessed within the case, combined with the downward sloping lug design, this piece wears much more like a typical 39-40mm timepiece. The bezel has a uni-directional rotating design and houses a black aluminum insert with individual minute markers. Inside, the dial features vibrant colored text and logos, along with Tritium plots and a high-contrast white-painted handset. Powering this piece is the robust workhorse Calibre 2824-2 by ETA. Last but not least, flip it over and you'll find the appropriate Military engravings denoting that it was property of the French Military. It is also accompanied by its decommission paper dating to 2003. This is a real piece of history — a phrase often repeated in the world of watches, though rarely as deservedly as in this case. And when compared to other military-issued pieces from other brands, particularly other dive watches issued to the Marine Nationale, this actually is fantastic value, and they do not grow on trees!

title: Omega Disco Volante Ref. CK2245 'UFO' - Black 'Gilt' Dial
description: Omega is undeniably one of the most historically important timepiece manufactures of all time. In fact, the Speedmaster is probably the most important wrist watch of all time. As a result, the Speedmaster casts a massive shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the Seamaster and Constellation ranges. The resulting effect is double sided: many vintage Omegas, we feel are incredibly undervalued in the market as it exists today, with the other side of that being that hidden gems are shocking attainable. Take the piece that we haver here, a stainless steel 'Disco Volante' time-only watch loaded with beautiful details. Dating to circa 1944, this Ref. CK2445 is also known as a 'UFO' for its 'hidden' lug design, making for case design that is reminiscent of a flying saucer. The case itself is made from stainless steel and comes in at a massive 39mm in diameter with a recessed crown and one of Omega's manual-winding movements inside. Despite the somewhat unusual appearance of the round design with no lugs, it must be said that the black dial is the highlight of this piece. It features a glossy black surface with a 'concentric' subsidiary seconds register at the 6 o'clock position, gold-tone 'Arabic' indices, an outer minute track, and a gold-tone 'syringe' handset typing it all together. This piece, with its sizing, condition, and design cues really embodies everything that makes vintage great. What more can you ask for?

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1603 - Sunburst Grey 'Sigma' Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a Reference 1603 from circa 1972 and it comes to us in strong overall condition, with a gently previously polished case, an 'engine-turned' steel bezel, and a matching Jubilee bracelet — all showing uniform normal wear. Inside, the sunburst grey 'Sigma' dial is beautifully preserved, retaining a crisp and vibrant sunburst finishing seemingly devoid of the usual degradation found on colored dials from this era. The Tritium plots remain fully-intact and show an attractive and even patina throughout with a handset that has ages a bit darker. All things considered, this is tough to beat, be it for your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Tudor Submariner Ref. 7016/0 - Black 'Snowflake'
description: The Submariner, namely those produced by Rolex, has long been considered the cream of the crop when it comes to watch collecting as a whole. Possibly the most iconic watch ever produced, the Submariner has long standing utilitarian roots that span decades, and everyone who’s anyone has been spotted wearing one. However, if you look deeper into the Submariner line, you may find a less known but just as incredible model manufactured by Tudor. These pieces are not only more unique and uncommon than the traditional Submariner, but offer a more fun, playful design — particularly with the blue-dialed variants like the example that we have here. This example, a Ref. 7016/0, dates to circa 1973 and is known as a 'Snowflake' for it's distinctive hands and indices. In recent years, these have developed a cult following with collectors and have become one of the more sought after and collectible vintage Tudor Submariner References. This particular example comes to us in strong overall condition, with a professionally refurbished Oyster case touting prominent chamfers and nice thick lugs. The bezel retains excellent factory definition and houses a black bezel insert that shows normal wear with a matching pip. Inside, the black dial presents very nicely, with the characteristic square Tritium plots show a light and uniform patina throughout, with the equally characteristic 'snowflake' handset matching the dial perfectly. It comes fitted with a correct, albeit slightly later Oyster bracelet with a signed fliplock clasp. These days, Tudors most popular line, the Black Bay, drawn largely from pieces like the one that we have here, and for good reason. As the expression goes, you can’t know where you’re going until you know where you’re from. This is a compelling example of a vintage diver that has seen steady grown in popularity, with no signs of stopping....

title: Jaeger-LeCoultre Polaris Memovox Ref. E859 - Single Family Owned
description: The Jaeger LeCoultre Polaris is the most complicated way to solve a problem - and that is why we love it! What is that problem? How do I know when I am going to run out of oxygen underwater! Decades before the Polaris, Jaeger LeCoultre has been producing its highly novel and unique alarm watch known as ‘The Memovox’. That model utilized and automatic winding in—house movement with a mechanical alarm function. At some point, this complication and design was thought to be married to a highly technical and robust diving watch that would be for the most serious of professionals. That watch, was the Polaris and its brother the Deep Sea Alarm. Both of those watches are icons today, but The Polaris is the most interesting of the two as it married the Alarm Memovox, with the Technical SuperCompressor case and internal rotating dive bezel to create a truly innovating and unique watch sporting three crowns. The top crown controlled your inner bezel, the middle time, and the bottom the alarm. All housed under a massive plexi dome crystal. The idea being that you could use the alarm to physically (as the watch does vibrate) and visibly (as it would emit bubbles underwater) alert you when you would be running out of air on a dive. Think about the technical prowess to build a waterproof dive watch with multiple inner rotating discs, operated by THREE crowns, and has a resonator case back… FULL OF HOLES! It's large size (by the standards of the time) lends for a perfect modern wearing experience and has become an icon of the JLC historical canon. The example that we have here comes to us from the family of the original owner, whom was in fact, a diver! The case, crystal, and dial shows signs of real use and wear, while remaining well preserved given the life it has lived. The case remains unpolished and shows honest wear, as does the crystal which is likely original to the watch. Even all three of the original and correct 'hashed' crowns remain. Inside, the dial is nicely preserved, with evenly patinated Tritium elements and some light surface patina. And then of course, there is the wildly cool and incredibly useful alarm function. The center section of the dial actually rotates counter-clockwise via the crown at the 2 o'clock position, and features an indicator in the form of Tritium triangle. Being a diver, it of course also features a rotating timing ring, but unlike a vast majority of dive watches with an externally-affixed rotating bezel, the Polaris utilizes a rotating inner ring in place of the chapter ring and is operated by the crown at 4 o'clock. These pieces are as beautiful as they are functional. A brilliant example of mid-century design through and through. And, the ultimate cooking watch.

title: Eberhard and Co. Pre Extra-Fort - Satin Silver 'Snail' Dial c. 1940
description: We've handled, collected, sold, and personally owned a number of Eberhards over the years, and it has become clear that each brings a distinctly different character to wrist. There's a consistent sense of individuality across the brands offerings and no two models feel quite the same. From the highly sought-after Scafograf, to the earlier and more obscure 'snail dial' chronographs, Eberhard's designs remain consistently engaging, each with a personality that sets it apart from the their contemporaries. This is not a manufacturer defined by restraint or uniformity, but rather by a willingness to experiment and specialize. The piece that we have here is a very special chronograph dating to circa 1940. Along with a handful of other chronographs that pre-date the Extra-Fort model that debuted in 1942, this is colloquially known as a 'Pre Extra-Fort.' It features a massive for the era, 40mm case crafted out of solid yellow gold with a 'hinged' caseback affixed to the left profile, fixed 'wire' lugs, a crown at 3 o'clock, and what appears to be a pair of 'oval' pushers in the usual configuration. The top pusher functions as a monopusher for the chronograph while the lower pushers is a locking/stop mechanism in disguise. Even today, this very unique function is thanks to one of the highest-grade chronograph movements of the era: Eberhard's Cal. 16000. Based on the Valjoux Cal. 65, this massive 36mm movement was and is about as Eberhard as Eberhard gets, truly embodying the ethos of the brand. The condition of this piece is fantastic — wonderfully-preserved throughout for a watch of this age, let alone a precious metal chronograph. The case remains strong with correct finishing and shows normal wear, with no apparent damage or major wear. The silver dial inside is also excellent, with a gentle patina across the surface, nicely-preserved printed scales and indices, and a blued-steel 'syringe' handset tying it all together. Best of all, it is an Eberhard. A brand unknown to many, but with models such as the Scientigraf, Scafograf, and Contograf, tug hard at the hearts of so many collectors of vintage. And like many Eberhards, these were produced in small numbers and are seldom-seen on the open market. This sold gold example, quite simply, is something we have never seen and very well may never seen again.

title: Breguet Empire 35mm - Silver 'Guilloché' Dial w/ Peseux 260 & Extract
description: Parisian manufacturer Breguet, named after its founder, Abraham-Louis Breguet, was founded in 1775 and is one of the most stored and historically significant manufacturers in the world of horology. With a number of firsts, including *ahem* what many consider to be the first known wristwatch, Breguet is primarily known today for its stunning silver 'guilloche' dials, innovations in complications, and outstanding build quality. The 35mm dress watch that we have here is something incredibly special and important. Called an 'Empire', it dates to circa 1969 and in addition to being rare in in its own right as all Breguet timepieces from this era are, it is both the condition of this particular example and the movement powering it that further adds to its horological significance. Coming in at the larger of two available sizes, 35mm in diameter, it features a very Breguet coin-edge case design with 'officer'-style lugs, and a snapback caseback, and a yellow gold crown. As with virtually all Breguet dress watches, the dial within is an absolute delight to behold, and this piece is no exception. Silver in color, it features a variety of guilloché finishing techniques, black printed indices, a subsidiary seconds register at the 6 o'clock position, and of course, a 'Breguet' handset executed in yellow gold. Simplicity executed on the highest level. The condition of this piece is exceptional. Seemingly spared of any previous polishing, it features strong factory finishing throughout, with clear hallmarks and engravings, and a beautifully preserved dial within — once again contributing to the attractiveness of this package. Last but not least, the movement inside. Designed specifically for Observatory chronometer competition trials to be as accurate as possible, the Peseux Cal. 260 is generally regarded as one of the finest time-only chronometer watch movements of the 20th century. It was produced for about 23 years with approximately 3,300 units made, and allegedly, never sold to the public. Instead, these were distributed to high-end brand such as Leroy, CYMA, and Breguet. Additionally, accompanying this piece is an extract from Breguet's archives confirming the original date of sale in 1969. We cannot overstate how special it is to be able to offer not only a stunning example of a rare and timeless watch, but one with supporting documentation like what we have here, and from one of the most prestigious brands on earth. How can you go wrong?

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 16018 - 'Onyx' Stone Dial Unpolished
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The 4-Digit Datejusts was the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials — something that has stuck with the Datejust name ever since. What the 4-digits watches do lack, is a quickset date — something that was resolved with the introduction of the 5-digit pieces in the late 1970s. There are levels to collecting. For starters, this is a solid-gold Datejust which are rare to begin with - Rolex did not make a lot of these so it didn’t compete with its more expensive sibling, the Day-Date, which were exclusively produced in solid gold. Not only is this one such example of a solid gold Datejust, but this also houses a factory stone dial. Throughout the years Rolex produced a number of highly exclusive, limited production, stone dials. These were dials made from shaved down pieces of Lapis Lazuli, Malachite, Coral, and in this case - Onyx. These dials were fragile and difficult to work with - but when they got it right they offer such depth and natural beauty it easy to see why collectors lust for these pieces. While these were also made as Day-Dates, we actually prefer the cleaner dial of the Datejust which allows for more of the stone to come through to a truly stunning effect. The piece that we have here, a Ref. 16018, features a black 'onyx' dial, which belongs to a family of watches produced with a series of rare and exotic stones, and are as rare as they are beautiful to behold. Produced by Rolex for a limited time, these dials were handmade by artisans — something we don't usually associate with Rolex and the sports watches that they are know for — and have always been coveted as some of the more collectible vintage Rolexes, full stop. This example dates to circa 1988 and is offered in strong overall condition, with a fantastic, unpolished Oyster case and 'fluted' yellow gold bezel. The stone dial within exhibits a faint vertical hairline fracture — hardly visible to the naked eye — along with a framed date aperture and a non-luminous yellow gold handset. This of course means that you can wear this one freely! While not the rarest of the stone dials, the variety of color ranging from gold to brown in the stone is always a pleaser and never short in demand. While not the rarest of the stone dials, the depth of the black Onyx is always a pleaser and never short in demand.

title: Heuer Autavia Ref. 2446 'Rindt' - Matte Black 'Reverse-Panda' Dial
description: While the Carrera gets all the attention, the Heuer Autavia is actually the ‘OG’ Heuer. A combination of ‘Automotive’ and ‘Aviation’ - the Autavia line originally started as dash mounted rally timers made for motorsport and aviation applications. It was not until the early 1960s that first Autavia wrist chronographs came around. The first generation Autvaia, the Reference 2446, utilized screw-back cases and the venerable Valjoux 72 manual-winding movements, while the second generation case with used a snap-back case or ‘Compressor’ Case - hence the model shift to 2446C. The watch that we have here is the former: a Ref. 2446 with a 'Second Execution' case and 'Third Execution' dial. In addition to the aforementioned screw-down caseback, it also features 'pump' pushers, a winding crown at 3 o'clock, and an externally-mounted bezel assembly — all mated to a wonderfully-sized 38mm case. This particular example dated to circa the late 1960s and is offered in excellent overall condition. The case retains symmetrical lugs at each corner, with clear factory facets, crisp undersides and shows normal wear. The bezel assembly and black 12-hr insert show matching wear and present beautifully. Inside, the dial features a desirable 'reverse-panda' layout, with its black base and contrasting white subsidiary registers with 'concentric' finishing within. It remains in fantastic overall condition, virtually free of wear or damage, with applied 'faceted' indices, gently patinated Tritium plots, and a matching handset. Since its conception, the Autaiva, in virtually all of its guises, has become one of the most desirable chronographs ever produced, and its not difficult to see why: Excellent, robust and proven movements, legible dial layouts, and they hail from one of the most storied brands to ever be associated with chronographs.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 16014 - Black Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The 4-Digit Datejusts was the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials — something that has stuck with the Datejust name ever since. What the 4-digits watches do lack, is a quickset date — something that was resolved with the introduction of the 5-digit pieces in the late 1970s. The piece that we have here, a Reference 16014 from circa 1982, comes to us with an excellent, gently and tastefully previously polished Oyster case with the correct 'fluted' white gold bezel seemingly spared of previous polished. Inside, the black dial presents nicely, with a deep glossy surface and evenly patinated Tritium plots with a matching handset. Of course, this piece also features a handy quickset date function and comes fitted to a correct solid-link Jubilee bracelet with a signed blade clasp. Black-dialed Datejusts are less common than you may think... And there is almost some Explorer-like sportiness about them, while of course, still being a Datejust. This one, like virtually any Datejust , can be your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus 'Midsize' Ref. 3800/1A - Blue 'Teak' Dial
description: The Nautilus. Another Gerald Genta horological icon, sibling to the Royal Oak, and conductor of the Hype Train. Now that we have that out of the way, how did a brand like Patek Philippe get so famous for a steel time-only watch? Well, by accident. The Stern family, which still owns Patek, was constantly being asked back in the late 60s to make a steel sports watch. It turns out that loyal collectors of the brand who would buy their high complication watches and precious metal dress pieces had become so loyal to Patek - that they would only wear wristwatches from the illustrious brand. Not one to disappoint their well-heeled clientele, Gerald Genta was commissioned to design a sports watch worthy of the Patek name. Much like the Royal Oak, the steel case was treated to a wide variety of complex finishing techniques normally reserved for precious metals. While this was a sports piece, it was still to be a Patek Philippe above all else. Unlike the far more rugged Royal Oak, the Nautilus has gentler curves - and certainly no exposed bolts or rivets (can you imagine!). What we have here is a Reference 3800/1A — the 'midsize' variant of the first Reference of Nautilus, the 3700. Coming in at 37mm in diameter, these pieces retain all of the exceptional looks, feel, and brand pedigree of the 'Jumbo' sibling, in a slightly more digestible package. This particular example comes to us in fantastic overall condition, with a professionally refurbished case and matching bracelet that shows only light wear from gentle use. It also features what is generally regarded. as the most desirable dial variant within, well, any Nautilus range: a blue 'teak' dial. Like the rest of the watch, it also remains in fantastic condition, seemingly devoid of the usual wear or flaking that is commonly found on colored dials from this era. The applied white gold Tritium-filled indices exhibit a light and even patina with a nicely matching handset. As the saying goes: "You never actually own a Patek Philippe. You merely look after it for the next generation." This one is ready for it's next lucky caretaker.

title: Rolex King Midas Ref. 4315 - 'Brushed' Champagne Dial W/ Hangtag
description: In the late 1960s, Rolex was looking to expand their lineup of watches with both more traditional designs, as well as design-forward offerings. This line of watches became known called the Cellini line with a subsidiary lineup called 'Midas.' Like the rest of the Cellini line, the Midas pieces would come in a wide variety of shapes, sizes, and dial options, and all in solid gold. The flagship offering within the Midas line, the 'King Midas' were amongst the most expensive models the brand had ever produced and, at the time, limited in their production. The piece that we have here is one of those watches, a King Midas Reference 4315. This very special piece features a five-sided case with a screw-down caseback, "King Midas" engraved into the left case profile, a truly integrated 'flat-link' bracelet with a 'hidden' deployant clasp, and a recessed crown at the 9 o'clock position styled to look like a sun. This particular yellow gold example dates to circa 1976 and is offered in excellent overall condition. The case and bracelet both show normal signs of wear from age with no notable damage or blemishes and no 'stretch.' The dial within features a 'brushed' texture on the champagne dial with an applied coronet logo, Cellini script on the bottom half, and a simple yellow gold stick handset. Most of the Cellini family features manual-winding movements, and this piece is no different. This then, is a brilliant example of Rolex displaying a more artistic side, all while very much being a Rolex at heart. Low production, precious materials, and its a Rolex. Hard to beat.

title: Omega 6B/542 Ref. 2777-1 - Matte Black 'Fat Arrow' Dial RAF-Issued Unpolished
description: Omega is undeniably one of the most historically important timepiece manufactures of all time. In fact, the Speedmaster is probably the most important wrist watch of all time. As a result, the Speedmaster casts a massive shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the Seamaster and Constellation ranges. The resulting effect is double sided: many vintage Omegas, we feel are incredibly undervalued in the market as it exists today, with the other side of that being that hidden gems are shocking attainable. The piece that we have here is special for a multitude of reasons. Not dissimilar to the 'Dirty Dozen' watches of WWII, this piece was commissioned by the British Ministry Of Defence to produce a watch that met a series of standards. Omega, along with a handful of other prominent watch manufacturers would rise to the challenge to produce a timepiece that had a certain level of resistance to shock, magnetism, dust, and of course, excellent timekeeping. Dating to circa 1953, this example is offered in fantastic overall condition. The 36mm case remains unpolished and shows normal wear with no notable damage or indication this ever really saw the action that it was intended... It features 'fixed' lug bars and a screw-down caseback with all of the correct engravings. No doubt the most intriguing element of the condition on this piece, is the dial. As a general rule with military watches, hands and dials were replaces under contract service, and as a result is accepted in the collector community. The result is that many military-issued piece prior to the 1960s no longer have their original dials with Radium paint, rather later dials with Tritium (this is where the 'Circle T' comes from). With the 6B/542, however, rather than a 'circle T' the MOD choose to denote the presence of Tritium on the new dials with a thicker 'fat' Broad Arrow. The dial itself presents nicely, showing light wear throughout with clear printing and evenly patinated Tritium elements and a correct Tritium 'sword' handset. This piece comes fitted to a very appropriate Admiralty Grey NATO strap from Phoenix and is powered by Omegas Cal. 283 manual-winding movement. Rumored to have only been produced for a year or two, there's no saying how many examples survive today, let alone in condition as well-rounded as this. To many collectors of vintage, regardless of whether the focus is of military watches or not, this piece has everything going for it. Military issued, properly vintage, and its from one of the most storied brands in the history of watchmaking. This is a real piece of history — a phrase often repeated in the world of watches, though rarely as deservedly as in this case.

title: Tudor Submariner Ref. 7928 'PCG' - Gilt 'Tropical' Dial
description: The Submariner, namely those produced by Rolex, has long been considered the cream of the crop when it comes to watch collecting as a whole. Possibly the most iconic watch ever produced, the Submariner has long standing utilitarian roots that span decades, and everyone who’s anyone has been spotted wearing one. However, if you look deeper into the Submariner line, you may find a less known but just as incredible model manufactured by Tudor. The Ref. 7928 that we have here dates to circa 1961 and is offered in strong overall condition. The case remains thick and symmetrical, with the 'pointed crown guards' clearly on display and factory chamfers visible. Inside, the glossy black 'gilt' dial has aged to various shades of brown, resulting in a wildly tropical patina. The luminous plots also shows patina from age and are complimented by a matching handset. The knurled bezel houses an excellent black 'fat font' insert with a patinated pip and it comes fitted to a slightly later 'stretch-rivet' Oyster bracelet with a blade clasp. For many of us, this is what vintage is all about: subtle details, honest condition that tells a story, and uniqueness in wear/patina. This one embodies all of the above!

title: Vacheron Constantin Rectangular Dress Watch Ref. 7139 - 'Brushed' Silver Dial
description: Vacheron Constantin can trace its roots back to 1755 and along with only a handful of other brands, is credited as one of the oldest manufacturers of mechanical clocks, pocket-watches, and of course, watches. In fact, Vacheron enjoys the prestige as the oldest continually operating manufacturer that still operates today. Vacheron is also a member of what has become known as The Holy Trinity , along with Patek Philippe and Audemars Piguet. All three of these manufactures have very different identities and focus areas within the industry, with VC generally regarded as the technical innovator. And despite a bevy of both technical and mechanical firsts, including the most complicated watch ever at the time of writing this, VC remains the lesser known name of the three in the broader watch community and certainly least understood. The piece that we have here is a yellow gold rectangular dress watch dating to circa 1960. The case comes in at 19mm x 29mm and remains in excellent condition, showing just normal wear with a gentle warmth to the gold. The dial inside is silver in color and features an elegant, vertically 'brushed' finishing with applied indices and is complimented by a matching 'pencil' handset. It comes fitted to a signed black alligator strap with a gold tone buckle and is powered by Vacheron's Calibre K1001/2 manual-winding movement. In some ways, this piece is very different for Vacheron. Highly restrained when it comes to eccentric, daring details and 'simple' in its design. That of course means, like other Swiss watches from this era, the execution and simplicity speaks for itself.

title: Rolex Submariner Ref. 5512 - 'Meters First'
description: The Rolex Submariner is a true icon — and the word "icon" does get thrown around an awful lot. If you were to ask ten people at random to draw you their idea of a watch looks like, chances are they would draw or describe something that looks like a Rolex Submariner. It’s the dive watch of reference, and good/bad/indifferent there is no escaping it. Throughout its 70-year production, there have been countless small changes made to the model, with the Reference 5512 representing a very interesting period in the Submariner story. The Ref. 5512 was originally sold alongside the 5513 as an up-market chronometer certified version of the venerable dive watch icon. During its production run, the 5512 series transitioned from the glossy gilt dials of the early 1960s, to matte dials in the later examples — as well as a bevy of different case and crown guard shapes. The piece that we have here is a matte dial example dating to circa 1967. It is known within the collector community as a 'Meters First' 5512 for its printing of the depth rating on the dial beginning with meters, followed by the equivalent in feet. This is the only execution of matte dials with this configuration. This example comes to us in strong overall condition, with a professionally refurbished Oyster case with those gorgeous chamfers clear and present and a 'rivet' Oyster bracelet with a blade clasp. The bezel assembly retains excellent definition and houses a gorgeous faded 'fat font' insert with a patinataed pip. Inside, the dial is beautifully-preserved, with a nice clean surface, gently patinated Tritium plots, and a handset that has aged slightly darker. For many of us, this is what vintage is all about: subtle details, honest condition that tells a story, and uniqueness in wear/patina. This one embodies all of the above!

title: Audemars Piguet 'Hinged-Lug' Dress Watch - Satin Silver Dial W/ Box
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. So, watches like the svelte and, frankly, stunning yellow gold dress watch that we have here offer offer not just a ton of value next to their iconic siblings, but were produced in relatively limited quantities. The piece that we have here is one of those pre-Royal Oak era watches: a rare yellow gold 'Tank'-style dress watch dating to circa the 1950s. Noticeable even at a glance, the lugs hint at their fully-articulating nature, with fine spacing between them and the case itself. When turned to profile view, the articulating nature of the lugs becomes apparent, as well as the intricate, sculpted finishing that they possess throughout. The bezel has a high-polish finish, framing the satin silver dial within. The dial itself shows honest signs of aging, with applied yellow gold 'dart' and 'Arabic' indices, a subsidiary seconds register on the lower half, and a yellow gold 'pencil' handset typing it all together. It is powered by a manual-winding movement by AP. Last but not least, this piece is accompanied by its box and comes fitted with a 'Saffiano'-textured brown leather strap with its original yellow gold signed buckle. This then, is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be. Only in the last few years have collectors and enthusiasts alike started to pay a bit more attention to pieces like these and, we think, its long overdue.

title: Oyster Watch Co. Oyster Junior Sport Ref. 2280F - 'Brushed' Silver Dial
description: The Oyster Watch Co. was born out of the same basic problem faced by many smaller watchmakers: producing a high-quality watch entirely in-house is expensive. The solution was to use reliable Swiss movements and pair them with well-made cases, dials, and other components. This allowed Oyster Watch Co. to offer an attractive, well-built watch at a much lower price-point. Sound a little bit like... Tudor? That would be a correct statement. Interestingly, or rather perplexingly, The Oyster Watch Co. was founded just two years after Tudor by the same person: Hans Wilsdorf. Like Wilsdorf's other brands, the Oyster Watch Co. designs often echoed the styles of one another, usually sharing names, parts, and even reference numbers. The piece that we have here, an Oyster Junior Sport, is a 'mid size' Oyster model that, as its name suggest, utilizes a water-resistant Oyster case along with a manually-wound movement, and nothing else. No frills — purely a functional timekeeping device. Dating to circa 1940, this example is offered in strong overall condition. The 30mm case remains thick and symmetrical, with a correct smooth steel bezel, and a screw-down crown. The silver dial within shows a light and uniform patina across the 'brushed' surface, with excellent black printed 'Arabic' indices, 'railroad' minute track, and text. The Radium luminous plots exhibit uniform darkening and the handset has been previously color-matched with Tritium and presents beautifully. It is believed that these Junior Sport models in particular were sold in the Canadian market, and were often found at military PXs. They were popular among soldiers in WWII for their water-resistance, robustness, and simplicity. All things considered, like many Oyster models from Rolex and Tudor in the 1940s-1950s, this piece remains not only slept on, but flat out unknown to the greater collecting community.

title: Heuer Carrera Ref. 7753NT - Matte Black Dial Unpolished Belgian Air Force-Issued
description: The Heuer Carrera has been called a perfect chronograph by many collectors and enthusiasts. Much like the Autavia that predates it, the Carrera had been intended to be a watch for auto racing — functional, legible, and reliable. Building on what are known as 'Pre-Carreras,' the first iteration to bear the 'Carrera' name on the dial, the Reference 2447N, would spawn a long line of watches that have been in almost continuous production right up until today. The aforementioned Ref. 2447N debuted in 1962, the same year as the Rolex Le Mans Ref. 6239 (changed to Daytona a year later in 1963) and both shared many of the same design characteristics: both featured a matte black 'reverse-panda' dial made by Singer, a stainless steel case that were very similar in size, and both utilized the venerable Valjoux 72 manual-winding chronograph movement within. In fact, the largest difference between the two at a glance is the execution of the tachymeter scales. The Carrera, like many successful model lines, would later see numerous other executions in the form of different movements, dials, etc., but these pieces with the now classic 36mm case remain the most coveted by collectors. The Carrera that we have here, a '30' Ref. 7753NT, was introduced in 1970 as a two-register alternative to the original 3-register Carrera, with the running-seconds register at the 9 o'clock position and a minute counter at the 3 o'clock position. These pieces utilized a manual-winding Valjoux Cal. 7730 movement and came in a number of dial variants — all within that classic 36mm case design. However, this is no ordinary Carrera... This particular 7753 features a unique configuration, with oversized 'Arabic' numerals painted in Tritium and a white-painted 'sword' handset with matching Tritium. If this configuration sounds familiar, thats is because this was a popular, almost universal standard for pilot's chronographs beginning in the 1930s. This piece is no different. Flip it over, and you'll find military engravings, revealing its connection to the Belgian Air Force. It is rumored that Belgium placed an order for these chronographs to be utilized by their Air Force in Africa during the wake of the Congo Crisis in the 1960s. These 200-250 pieces would have been delivered in roughly 1970 and it is estimated that only a handful survive today. It must be said that out of the very small number of these that are around today, this must be the finest example ever to surface. The case remains unpolished, with strong, defined finishing on those characteristic 'faceted' lugs, 'pump' pushers, a signed crown, and clear military engravings on the caseback. The dial inside, is beautifully-preserved, with a nice black surface, clear printing throughout, and evenly patinated Tritium elements. Since its conception in the early 1960s, the Carrera has become one of the most desirable chronographs ever produced, and its not difficult to see why: Excellent, robust and proven movements. Simple, legible dial layouts. And of course, that striking, unmistakable case with virtually perfect proportions, for nearly any wrist. To many collectors of vintage, regardless of whether the focus is of military watches or not, this chronograph has everything going for it. Military issued, properly vintage, fantastic condition, and its a Heuer. What more does one need?

title: Patek Philippe Rose Gold Dress Watch Ref. 1450 'Top Hat' - 'Brushed' Silver Dial Unpolished
description: As far as brand identity goes, Patek Philippe, unlike many brands, is seemingly free of being associated with any one model in particular, and instead enjoys a reputation for quality, craftsmanship, and a long-standing pedigree as a top Swiss manufacturer. Of course, there are models and model families that are nothing short of icons (e.g., Nautilus, Calatrava, Grand Complications, etc.) but if you dig deep enough there are hidden gems that do not even fall into any of these families. Take the rectangular dress watch that we have here for example. Dating to circa 1948, this piece is perfectly emblematic of a new era of design coming out of Switzerland from this era. Beautifully-sized at 21mm x 37mm, it features a 'hooded' lug design, with a widened top and bottom case and 'hidden' case profile. It's nickname, 'Top Hat' is drawn form the resulting appearance of the unique case design. The solid rose gold case itself remains in excellent overall condition and houses a 'brushed' silver dial with applied rose gold indices and a matching rose gold 'pencil' handset. It is powered by one of Patek's manual-winding calibres via the signed rose gold crown at 3 o'clock. Lesser-known than model lines like the Calatrava, complicated chronographs, and the Ellipse, Patek's from the earlier part of the twentieth century into the middle of the century offer surprisingly good value relative to their more established successors. This piece is one of the more unique designs that we have had the pleasure of offering on the website.

title: Abercrombie & Fitch Co. Seafarer Ref. 2443 'Second Execution' - Silver Dial Unpolished
description: Abercrombie & Fitch Co., long before its modern reinvention, was one of America’s preeminent sporting outfitters. From its midtown Manhattan flagship, the firm supplied serious outdoorsmen with the finest equipment available, often commissioning bespoke products from respected manufacturers to meet the specific demands of its clientele. Watches were no exception. By the mid-20th century, A&F had begun offering co-branded timepieces tailored to sportsmen, and when customers began requesting a watch capable of tracking the tides, the company turned to one Charles-Edouard Heuer to bring the idea to life. Commissioned at A&F’s request, the Solunar was introduced in 1949 and advertised as the only watch to display both 'Solar' and 'Lunar' time. Produced in a limited run of just around 1,000 pieces, it was a highly specialized instrument and ultimately a niche offering. Still, its innovation laid the groundwork for the Seafarer, which paired the original tidal display with one of Heuer’s signature complications: the chronograph. Retaining traditional hour and minute counters, the Seafarer replaced the running seconds register with a tide indicator at 9 o’clock, which was directly adjustable via a left-side pusher and synchronized using published tide tables. Produced from the 1950s through the 1970s in several case configurations shared with other Heuer chronographs, the Seafarer remained a distinctive but specialized entry within the broader catalog and saw a handful of different variations over that time. The example that we have here, a Ref. 2443, dates to the 1950s and is offered in excellent, beautifully-preserved condition. The case comes in at 38mm in diameter and features nice thick lugs with sharp undersides, along with small 'pump' pushers, and a 'stepped' top case. Inside, the silver dial shows light aging throughout, retaining nice colors in within the subsidiary registers and beautiful gold 'foil' indices with a correct gold-tone handset. The movement powering this piece is a modified version of the famous Valjoux 72 which of course, is manually-wound. For the most part, all Abercrombie & Fitch Co. timepieces have become collectible to an extent, but it is the Seafarer that is at the front of the pack in both desirability and collectability. This is the first time we have had the pleasure of offering on for sale on the website and we could not be more happy about it.

title: Audemars Piguet White Gold Dress Watch Ref. 5259 - Silver Dial w/ Box & Papers
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. And this is after considering that prior to the Royal Oak, AP made far fewer watches to start with... The piece that we have here is one of those pre-Royal Oak era watches: an ultra-thin dress watch dating to circa the 1960s. Nicely-sized at 33.5mm in diameter, the case is constructed out of white gold with an attractive 'linen' finishing on the top-case, a white gold crown, and a matching white gold 'mesh' bracelet with a signed locking clasp. Inside, the silver dial inside is very of-its-era, with simple printed "Audemars Piguet" script, elongated 'stick' indices, and a 'pencil' handset to match. This svelte piece is powered by AP's ultra-thin Calibre 2001 manual-winding movement. Last but not least, this piece is accompanied by its box, certificate of origin, and even the outer paper sleeve for the box. A very rare find. This then, is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be. Only in the last few years have collectors and enthusiasts alike started to pay a bit more attention to pieces like these and, we think, its long overdue.

title: Rolex Precision 'Grasshopper' Ref. 4560 - Satin Silver Dial
description: The 1950s was a decade that Rolex was really coming into their own. The 'Professional' line was almost immediately successful, giving the brand the capital to experiment and expand. The variety in metals, dials, and handsets in this era, particularly in the Oyster Perpetual, Oyster Precision, Datejust, and Day-Date families of watches was vast. It was also a time where the brand was playing around with manual-winding dress watches, usually denoted with 'Precision' on the dial. The piece that we have here comes from the 'Precision' family of watches and is without a doubt one of the more stylistic piece from the model family. Distinguished by its oversized, eccentric lugs, this and similar pieces have been dubbed by collectors as 'grasshopper' lugs — not dissimilar to 'horn', 'flame', or 'claw' lugs. Dating to circa 1946, the case comes in at nicely sized 34mm in diameter, but the sheer size of the lugs as they relate to the case lends itself to a wearing experience that resembles something closer to a 36mm diameter watch. It remains in very nicely overall condition, showing normal signs of wear throughout with symmetrical lugs and visible engravings on the caseback. The dial inside is as gorgeous as the case. Silver in color, it features a satin surface with both printed and silver 'foil' indices, a 'concentric' subsidiary seconds register, and a 'domed' shape all together. Of course, it is powered by a manual-winding mvoement. There is no doubt whatsoever that the Precision range remains an overlooked and interesting part of Rolex's history. Their artistic side. Pieces like this remind us that Rolex was once capable of deviating from the designs that they eventually became known for. If a Rolex were to be a Vacheron from this era, this is it.

title: Bucherer Chronograph Ref. 805-2 - 'Tropical' Silver Dial w/ Lemaina Cal. 2520 Unpolished
description: Bucherer is perhaps best known today as one of Switzerland’s most prominent luxury watch and jewelry retailers, but the company’s history stretches back more than a century. Founded in 1888 in Lucerne by Carl Friedrich Bucherer and his wife Louise, the firm built its reputation on quality, craftsmanship, and an intimate understanding of Switzerland’s developing watch industry. By the early twentieth century, Bucherer had become an important retailer for many of Switzerland’s leading watchmakers. In 1924, the company established its long-standing relationship with Rolex, becoming one of the brand’s earliest and most important retail partners. Like other prestigious retailers of the era, Bucherer also developed watches under its own name, as well as branded other manufacturers' watches as their own. Eventually, this gave rise to the Carl F. Bucherer brand that we have today. The piece that we have here is dates to circa the 1950s and possesses many of what makes some of the most iconic chronographs from this era great. The case comes in at 35mm in diameter and features gorgeous chamfered lugs, ‘pump’ pushers, a screw-down caseback, and a signed crown. The dial inside, once silver in color, has developed an intense and largely uniform 'copper' patina over the years, making for a completely unique piece. It has minimal script on the top half with Bucherer's logo and name, 'concentric' subsidiary registers, applied rose gold-tone indices that alternate from 'dart’ to 'Arabic' style, and a rose gold-tone 'Alpha' handset typing it all together. Perhaps the most noteworthy aspect of this watch, however, is the movement inside. Powering this piece is the Lemania Cal. 2520, which is essentially the same movement as the iconic and significant Omega Calibre .321. Chronographs from roughly the 1940s through the 1970s are, for many, thought of as the essence of what makes vintage watches cool. Many of these models and brands have ascended to an unattainable level, making for completely under-the-radar finds like this quite rare. We think it’s awesome, and we’re confident we’re not the only ones.

title: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Ref. 25654BA - Satin Champagne Dial Full Set
description: It’s not unfair to say that Audemars Piguet Royal Oak is one of the most iconic watches ever made. Designed in 1972 by Gerald Genta, the Royal Oak completely changed the way that we look at a steel sports watch. For the first time, stainless steel was treated as a precious metal - receiving complex finishing techniques of brushing, polishing, and beveling - all by hand. The idea that its eight hexagonal bezel screws would be finely finished and left exposed for the wearer to see was a revolutionary thought. It’s no surprise that the model became the calling card for the family owned Audemars Piguet - not to mention one of the most sought after watches in the world. While the initial 5402 was time-only, AP quickly began to capitalize on the success of the Royal Oak and begin to integrate other complications and variations into this case. Prior to the Royal Oak’s introduction, AP was a master of high complications making beautiful movements in precious metals. It was only a matter of time after the introduction of the Royal Oak that AP would continue to leverage that mastery and marry them with the new design. Which leads us to the Royal Oak that we have here, a Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Reference 25654BA. These pieces feature extremely similar proportions to the original 'Jumbo' Ref. 5402, albeit with a slightly thicker (or rather, less thin) case due to the movement within. Otherwise, that iconic integrated bracelet, the hexagonal crown, octagonal bezel, and even a automatic-winding movement are all very familiar. This example is a tone-on-tone, solid yellow gold variant with a champagne dial inside. It is offered in fantastic condition, with a case and bracelet that seem to be devoid of any noteworthy previous polishing, an immaculate dial within, and a replacement deployant clasp. Additionally, this piece is accompanied by its outer box, inner winding box, booklets, serialized leather hangtag, corrector, winding key, and guarantee papers. Far rarer and more complicated than its standard 'Jumbo' predecessor, these QP Royal Oaks from the late 1980s-1990s still remain something of a bargain on the market today... ... One thing is for sure, thats usually an indication that it wont be the case forever...

title: Universal Genève Polerouter Ref. 20357/1 - Gilt 'Tropical' Dial Unpolished
description: Universal Genève was one of the many great brands that succumbed to the quartz crisis of the 1970s. While they disappeared, it was not for their lack of impressive watches. To underscore that fact, the Henri Stern Watch Agency in their nearly 80-year history has only ever sold two brands: Patek Philippe, and Universal Genève. One of, if not the model line that UG is best known for, is the Polerouter. Born from the genius of a young, 23-year old Gérald Genta — long before his name became synonymous with icons — the Polerouter is a watch that speaks to both the soul and the mind of the collector. Originally conceived to commemorate SAS’s pioneering flights over the north pole from Copenhagen to Los Angeles, it’s far more than a handsome vintage piece; it’s a true milestone in mid-century horology. With its distinctive aesthetic, refined movement, and enduring legacy, the Polerouter checks all of the boxes for the vintage connoisseur — a surprisingly rare occurrence. The example that we have here dates to circa 1959 and is probably very close to what comes to mind when you hear "Polerouter." It features a 33.5mm case with the characteristic 'twisted' lugs, a signed crown, and a screw-down caseback with the 'SAS polar route' engraving. Inside, the dial is framed with another Polerouter signature design characteristic: the engine-turned steel chapter ring. The dial itself is a correct black 'gilt' unit, with luminous plots present at all positions and a correct 'dauphine' handset to match. All of these details are textbook Polerouter and a delight to behold, but it must be said that it is the dial in this example that is the real highlight... Originally glossy black in color, it has aged to a gorgeous and even brown tone, resulting in a stunning 'tropical' patina. The surface retains its beautiful 'crosshair,' text, and equally beautiful applied 'sheild' logo at the 12 o'clock position. This piece is powered by what is probably the most desirable movement found in any Polerouter: an automatic-winding 'micro rotor' movement. UG was able to design a movement with the 'Microtor' embedded into the movement architecture, which results in a movement that is self-winding, but also thin. This is yet another Polerouter hallmark: they are thin. It is the culmination of details like the dynamic and perfectly-sized case, the dial layout with the asymmetrical date aperture, the efficient and innovative movement design, and the fantastic build quality that clearly show why Universal Genève is considered to be one of the finest manufactures in the era. ...and its only once it's on your wrist, that these details become apparent. They keep on delivering and continue to impress no matter what else might finds its way into your collection.

title: Rolex Explorer I Ref. 1016 - 'Frog Foot' Dial
description: May 29, 1953 After an arduous journey starting on March 10th of 1953, and an extremely difficult assault on the summit, Tenzing Norgay and Sir Edmund Hillary became the first people to successfully summit Mt. Everest. On their wrist? NOT a Rolex Explorer. Whoops. Well, to be fair the Rolex Explorer wasn’t created yet. So why the hullabaloo about Sir Edmund Hillary? Well - he was wearing a Rolex. A Rolex Oyster Perpetual. After hearing of the success of this expedition and ruggedness of the watch - the decision was made to replace the Oyster Perpetual with a new model named in Hillary’s honor - The Explorer. Or so the story goes. Either way, the Rolex Explorer I was introduced in 1953 but like many Rolex models, the first series was not considered ‘the best’ reference. For many collectors - the ultimate Explorer I is the reference 1016. It’s clean, highly legible and still tough enough for use in modern day wear. While using the same case as a Datejust, the smooth bezel and applied luminous Arabic 3,6,9 lend a more rugged and utilitarian aesthetic to the watch. Early models were made with gilt dials, which is when the lettering and fonts are punched out of the dial so that the brass ‘gilt’ color shows through creating a golden text appearance. These are not very easy to produce and were ultimately discontinued by Rolex in the later half of the 1960s as they couldn’t be produced in the same quantity as a matte dial - but nothing shines and glows like a Rolex gilt dial. The particular example that we have here is an early matte-dial example dating to circa 1967. It comes to us in fantastic overall condition, with a professionally-refurbished case and 'smooth' steel bezel that show light signs of wear throughout, fitted to a folded-link Oyster bracelet with a blade clasp. Inside, the dial is known to collectors as a 'Frog Foot' for the, well, frog-foot shape of the Rolex coronet at the 12 o'clock position. It remains in exceptional, beautifully-preserved condition with a nice clean surface, evenly patinated indices, and a matching handset. This is a phenomenal example of what many enthusiasts consider to be a perfect watch, and they simply do not surface often in condition like this.

title: Audemars Piguet Steel Dress Watch Ref. 5273 - 'Brushed' Blue Dial Unpolished
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. The piece that we have here is a very attractive stainless steel dress from circa the 1970s. On the surface, it is very simple. The round case measures 34mm in diameter with turned down lugs, a crown at 3 o'clock, and thats about it. Rotate it to a profile view, and it becomes apparent that this piece is incredible svelte considering it is automatic-winding. In fact it is powered by AP's Cal. 2120 — the very same movement used in the original 'Jumbo' Royal Oaks. Additionally, the dial is a gorgeous, very rare blue variant. The surface features a horizontally 'brushed' surface with minimal text, applied 'stick' indices, and a simple 'pencil' handset. This then, is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be.
