title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 1803 - Champagne 'Linen Non-Luminous' Dial Unpolished W/ Box & Papers
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Dwight D. Eisenhower was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a leather strap with a matching gold buckle, but also on a solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), like the example that we have here. The piece that we have here, a Reference 1803 from circa 1972, is a fantastic example finished in solid yellow gold with a gorgeous dial within. The case and characteristic 'fluted' bezel both seem to have been spared of previous polishing and present beautifully. Inside, the champagne dial features a lovely 'linen' texture on the surface remains in immaculate, seemingly flawless condition with its matching non-luminous handset. It comes fitted to it correct, albeit slightly earlier yellow gold 'President' bracelet with a blade clasp. Additionally, this piece is accompanied by its box and papers. This 1803 is nothing short of exceptional. Any watch from this era in condition like this is a treat.... A Day-Date in yellow gold with an interesting dial is a dream.

title: Eterna KonTiki Ref. 130T - Sunburst Silver 'Domed' Dial Unpolished W/ Box
description: Eterna was founded in 1856 in Grenchen, Switzerland, by schoolteacher Dr. Josef Girard and Urs Schild, beginning life as a small movement manufacturer. By the early twentieth century, the company had established itself as one of the industry's leading manufactures, producing both complete watches and high-quality calibres for other brands. The brands greatest contribution came in 1948 with the introduction of the five-ball-bearing rotor, a seemingly simple innovation that dramatically improved the efficiency and longevity of automatic movements. The design became so closely associated with the company that five balls were incorporated into the Eterna logo, and the principle has since become a standard feature of automatic watchmaking across the industry. The piece that we have here comes from Eterna's 'KonTiki' family of watches and dates to circa 1963. It features a lovely, 'twisted-lug' steel case with a screw-down caseback, a crown at 3 o’clock, and a very attractive ‘domed’ dial within. Silver in color, it has a crisp sunburst surface with applied indices, patinated luminous plots, and a ‘dauphine’ handset. Last but not least, it comes fitted to a signed navy blue suede strap with a signed steel buckle and a box. Eterna offers strong value in the world of vintage, and a package like this in fantastic condition is always a plus!

title: Movado 'Calatrava' Ref. 18610 - Silver 'Sector' Dial Unpolished
description: While it may be hard to imagine based upon their product line today, Movado Factories (yes, that was the full name) once made watches that were beautifully designed, exceptionally-well made, and respected on a level that matched the very best manufacturers. Some of their more sought-after models include the M90 and M95 chronographs of the 1940s - 1970s, the Sub-Sea range, and both time-only and complicated pieces that utilized case designs shared with brands like Patek Philippe, Mido, and DOXA. The watch that we have, a Sport Ref. 18136 from circa the 1940s, is one of the latter 'waterproof' models that shares a similar design and in fact, the same case-maker as properly heavy hitting references from this era. That is, of course, François Borgel. The case itself is a 30mm in diameter and features very attractive 'stepped' finishing on the top case, with dynamic, faceted lugs, a screw-down caseback, and a 'domed' crown . Its simple 'calatrava'-style design is as attractive as ever, and with a silver dial inside, versatile as well. Naturally, it shows signs of aging with a light patina throughout and presents beautifully. Adding to the appeal are the patinated 'Arabic' indices, matching blued-steel handset, and that red-tipped seconds hand. Last but not least, powering this piece is Movado's own Calibre 260 manual-winding movement. In our opinion, and we know there are a handful of other dealers and enthusiasts out there that share this viewpoint, there are not many brands that get design this right. Simple as that. Simple, timeless elegance. Not many brands can do it better...

title: Rolex Oyster Perpetual Date Ref. 1501 - Blue 'Mosaic' Dial
description: If you boil Rolex down to its purest form, what do you get? The Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is truly the genesis for the entire Rolex brand. The very first Rolex models were called ‘Oysters’ which was owed to their innovative three part case that all screwed into each-other. That is where the fluted bezel actually derives from, being screwed down into the top of the case to secure the crystal with a gasket - as well as the grooves on the oyster case back. All makes sense now - right? The piece that we have here, simply known as an Oyster Perpetual Date , is a descendant of those early watches, utilizing a water-resistant Oyster case, an automatic-winding movement, and a date complication. A functional, sturdy, and dependable timekeeping device. Dating to circa 1971, this Reference 1501 features a 34mm Oyster case with a 'rivet' Oyster bracelet, and a unique to this reference, 'engine-turned' steel bezel. The case and bracelet have been very lightly previously polished and present beautifully, while the bezel has seemingly been spared of any previous polishing. Inside, the captivating blue 'mosaic' dial shows only faint degradation around the center post and edge, and retains a rich, vibrant blue color throughout. The Tritium plots and handset are all evenly patinated. The Oyster Perpetual line presents great value next to its slightly larger Datejust siblings, while simultaneously representing the essence of Rolex. This example, with that wildly cool dial, is not just a great entry point to a vintage Rolex, but could easily be your one vintage watch.

title: Rolex Submariner Date Ref. 1680 - 'Red Sub' MK4 Dial
description: The Rolex Submariner is a true icon — and the word "icon" does get thrown around an awful lot. If you were to ask ten people at random to draw you their idea of what a watch looks like, there is a significant chance that they would draw or describe something that looks like a Rolex Submariner. It’s the dive watch of reference, and good/bad/indifferent there is no escaping it. Throughout its 70-year production, there have been countless small changes made to the model, particularly in the first decade or so, with the 1680 representing a true landmark in the history of the model. The Ref. 1680 was the first Submariner to feature a date and enjoyed a long production run spanning close to 15 years. Why would a dive watch need a date? Well, this was the first step in marketing a tool watch beyond the diving community and crowd - because you definitely do not need to know the date underwater! The 1680 started a shift to civilian friendly models, and to this day, the Submariner Date outsells and outnumbers its 'no-date' sibling something like 10-1. Purity aside, this does make sense for most buyers. It utilizes the iconic Rolex cyclops married with the date function, yet remains clean and functional as ever. The piece that we have here, however, is no run of the mill Ref. 1680... This piece features a line of text on the dial that reads: “Submariner” in red, rather than the usual white. It has since become known to collectors as the "Red Sub." The example that we have here dates to circa 1970 and comes to us in honest overall condition. It features a tastefully previously polished case with symmetrical lugs and shows light signs of wear throughout no damage of note. The 'MK4' dial is fantastic. The matte surface remains clean and seemingly devoid of any major wear or damage, with evenly patinated Tritium plots and a matching handset. The 'fat font' bezel insert has faded to an attractive 'charcoal' with some patina visible on the markers themselves as well. It comes fitted to a correct, albeit later Oyster bracelet with a fliplock clasp. This piece offers compelling value in the world of 'Red Submariners' and makes for an excellent daily driver.

title: Smiths De Luxe Ref. 6B/542 - Matte Black 'Broad Arrow' Dial RAF-Issued Unpolished
description: Smiths can trace its origins to London in 1851, when Samuel Smith established a family business specializing in precision instruments and clocks. Over the following century, the company grew into one of Britain's foremost engineering firms, producing everything from automotive gauges to aircraft instruments before turning its attention to wristwatches. By the mid-twentieth century, Smiths was assembling watches in Wales using domestically produced movements, making them among the last truly British-made mechanical watches of their era. That reputation was cemented in 1953, when a Smiths wristwatch accompanied Sir Edmund Hillary on the first successful ascent of Mount Everest. The influx of inexpensive Swiss competition and the Quartz Crisis of the 1970s gradually brought Smiths' watchmaking ambitions to an end, with production ceasing by the early 1980s as the company refocused on its industrial and automotive businesses. Though the original watch division disappeared, the Smiths name has since been revived by Timefactors, whose faithful recreations preserve the utilitarian design, robust engineering, and distinctly British character that defined the marque's mechanical watches. The piece that we have here is special for a multitude of reasons. It was designed to meet the requirements of the British Ministry Of Defence to produce a watch that met a series of standards. Smiths, along with eleven other manufacturers would rise to the challenge to produce a timepiece that had a certain level of resistance to shock, magnetism, dust, and of course, excellent timekeeping. This example dates to circa 1965, which was the last year that these were produced and only very few were ever delivered. It is estimated that this is one of only about 300 units. The condition of this piece is extraordinary. The 36mm case remains unpolished and shows normal wear with no notable damage or indication this ever really saw the action that it was intended... The crown is probably original and the caseback retains all of the correct engravings. No doubt the most intriguing element of the condition on this piece, is the dial. As a general rule with military watches, hands and dials were replaces under contract service, and as a result is accepted in the collector community. The result is that many military-issued piece prior to the 1960s no longer have their original dials with Radium paint, rather later dials with Tritium (this is where the 'Circle T' comes from). This piece, however, has seemingly escaped contract service and retains its original Radium dial. Thankfully, like the rest of the watch, it remains is outstanding overall condition. The matte black surface is exceptionally clean and devoid of any major wear and retains excellent text and printing. The lower half bears the desirable 'Broad Arrow' and the Radium plots remain present and evenly paitnated with a correct and matching white-painted 'sword' handset Powering this piece is a British-made Calibre 27.CS manual-winding movements and comes fitted to a very appropriate green NATO strap. To many collectors of vintage, regardless of whether the focus is of military watches or not, this piece has everything going for it. Military issued, properly vintage, and borderline unbeatable condition. This is a real piece of history — a phrase often repeated in the world of watches, though rarely as deservedly as in this case.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1600 - Matte Black Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a Reference 1600 from circa 1969 and it comes to us in strong overall condition. The case has been tastefully previously unpolished and shows only light signs of wear throughout with symmetrical proportions. The smooth stainless steel bezel is also lightly previously polished and shows matching light wear. The dial inside, black in color, features a matte surface with very uncommon silver text, rather than the usual white. It is very nicely preserved with only faint edge wear, nicely patinated Tritium plots, and a matching handset. It comes fitted to a Jubilee bracelet with a blade clasp. Black-dialed Datejusts are less common than you may think... And there is almost some Explorer-like sportiness about them, while of course, still being a Datejust. That is to say, like any 4-digit Datejust, it can be your one vintage watch, or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Lemania Field Watch Ref. 203-4 - 'Brushed' Silver Dial
description: Lemania can trace its roots back to the Vallée de Joux, where it was founded in 1884 by Alfred Lugrin, a former Jaeger-LeCoultre craftsman with a talent for complicated movements. Operating first under his own name, Lugrin built a modest but formidable reputation through his chronograph work before his son-in-law Marius Meylan took the reins around 1930 and renamed the company Lemania. Survival through the Great Depression came by joining forces with Omega and Tissot in 1932, and it was within the newly-formed alliance that Lemania's true legacy was forged: Every Omega chronograph movement for the next four decades, including the the iconic Calibre .321, would be supplied or closely based off Lemania calibres. The Quartz Crisis of the 1970s nearly unravelled it all, and by 1981 Lemania had separated from the group and reborn itself as Nouvelle Lemania. A decade later, Breguet brought it into the fold, and when the Swatch Group absorbed Breguet in 1999, the Lemania name was quietly retired — though its workshops now forming movements for Manufacture Breguet. The piece that we have here is a field watch from circa the 1950s. The case measures a nice 33mm in diameter and has 'fixed'-bar lugs, a screw-down caseback, and Lemania's Calibre 3050 manual-winding movement. The silver dial inside has developed a nice, uniform patina across the 'brushed' surface, with patinated 'Arabic' indices, a clean 'concentric' subsidiary register on the lower half, and a matching blued-steel 'kite' handset to tie it all together. All things considered, this is a lovely, versatile vintage watch that can be worn by virtually anyone, and just happens to come from a great brand.

title: Movado 'Ladies' Octagonal 'Cocktail' Chronometer - 'Brushed' Silver 'Breguet' Dial LNOS
description: While it may be hard to imagine based upon their product line today, Movado Factories (yes, that was the full name) once made watches that were beautifully designed, exceptionally-well made, and respected on a level that matched the very best manufacturers. Some of their more sought-after models include the M90 and M95 chronographs of the 1940s - 1970s, the Sub-Sea range, and both time-only and complicated pieces that utilized case designs shared with brands like Patek Philippe, Mido, and DOXA. Those are all great models. We love them, and even collect them, but it allows for lesser-known pieces to slide through the cracks for most collectors... Take the watch that we have here for example: a ladies 'chronometer' dress watch from the 1940s. Offered in like new old stock condition, it features an octagonal 21mm x 21mm case with a crown at 3 o'clock, a snapback case, and a beautiful 'hourglass' leather strap with a steel buckle. It even retains its factory caseback sticker — though it shows some fade from age. The dial inside is exactly what you'd hope to find from Movado from this era... Silver in color, the surface is garnished with gold-tone 'Breguet' indices, a subsidiary seconds register at 6 o'clock, and a blued-steel 'sword' handset to tie everything together. Powering this piece is one of Movado's own manual-winding movements, which surprisingly, they've actually put through the chronometer certification paces as denoted on the dial with the chronometer text. In our opinion, and we know there are a handful of other dealers and enthusiasts out there that share this viewpoint, there are not many brands that get design this right. Simple as that.

title: Longines WWW 'Greenlander' Ref. 23088 - Matte Black 'Broad Arrow' Dial
description: Longines is one of the most well respected manufacturers of the 20th century, full stop. Founded in 1832 in Saint-Imier, Switzerland, the company built a name for themselves early on as a manufacturer of quality in-house movements right from the start. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Longines also built a reputation for precision timekeeping, earning accolades at international exhibitions and becoming a trusted name in sports timing, particularly in horse racing and aviation — an association with continues until today. By the mid-20th century, especially from the 1930s to the 1960s, Longines was at the peak of its technical and aesthetic prowess, producing a range of high-grade wristwatches admired today by collectors and vintage enthusiasts. The brand was known for its beautifully finished in-house movements, such as the 13ZN and 30CH chronographs, which are considered some of the finest column-wheel chronographs ever produced. The piece that we have here, a 'WWW,' dates to circa 1945 and is apart of a series of twelve watches that were was born out of the necessity of the British Ministry Of Defence to produce a watch that met a series of standards. Longines was one of the companies that would rise to the challenge to produce a timepiece that had a certain level of resistance to shock, magnetism, dust, and of course, excellent timekeeping. The name 'Greenlander' was initially tied to a claimed role in the 1952-54 British North Greenland Expedition, but has since since been debunked. The nickname, however, endures. Even without a Greenland expedition to its name, plenty of Longines watches saw real service on other missions through brutal Arctic conditions. Given that these watches were built for combat in the first place, the missing expedition does nothing to diminish the watch's pedigree. Battlefield or frozen frontier, the 'Greenlander' was engineered to hold up against either. The example that we have here is offered in honest overall condition, with a very nice 36mm case retaining excellent (and attractive) 'stepped' finishing on the top case and nice thick lugs that gently slope downward. The matte black dial inside shows some wear and patina from age, unsurprising given the life that was intended for the piece, and bears the desirable 'Broad Arrow' on the top half with an oversized subsidiary register on the bottom. It is powered by one of Longines' own Calibre 12.68Z manual-winding movements and comes fitted to a fantastic re-production single-pass textile strap. To many collectors of vintage, regardless of whether the focus is of military watches or not, this piece has everything going for it. Military issued, properly vintage, and its from one of the great brands. This is a real piece of history — a phrase often repeated in the world of watches, though rarely as deservedly as in this case.

title: Patek Philippe Gondolo Ref. 5024/1J - White 'Breguet' Dial
description: As far as brand identity goes, Patek Philippe, unlike many brands, is seemingly free of being associated with any one model in particular, and instead enjoys a reputation for quality, craftsmanship, and a long-standing pedigree as a top Swiss manufacturer. Of course, there are models and model families that are nothing short of icons (e.g., Nautilus, Calatrava, Grand Complications, etc.) but if you dig deep enough there are hidden gems that do not even fall into any of these families. Take the Gondolo line, for example. Largely overlooked by the broader watch community, this family of watches represents decades of elegant, design-forward pieces dating back nearly 100-years. The piece that we have here is a Reference 5024/1J from circa the 1990s. The case measures a substantial 30mm x 38mm and is crafted out of solid yellow gold with a matching five-link yellow gold bracelet. It has a signed, recessed crown at 3 o'clock, a sapphire crystal, and a curved caseback — allowing for an extremely comfortable wearing experience despite its mass. The case is reminiscent of 'Art Deco' pieces from the first half of the twentieth century, namely 'skyscraper' watches, with the stepped, rectangular design. Inside, the dial features high-contrast, black painted 'Breguet' indices on a stark white surface with a 'railroad' minute track, a subsidiary seconds register, and a matching black-painted 'feuille' handset. It is powered by Patek's proven Cal. 215 manual-winding movement. If you are looking for an alternative to something like a Santos, or maybe a Calatrava or complications aren't for you, then have a close look at this piece!

title: Audemars Piguet Cobra Ref. 5403BC - Sunburst Blue Dial
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. And this is after considering that prior to the Royal Oak, AP made far fewer watches to start with... The piece that we have here hails from circa the 1970s, an era when brands like Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Piaget, and even Rolex were experimenting with design-forward timepieces focused on finishing and opulence. The piece that we have here, colloquially known as a ‘Cobra’ for its woven, serpent-like construction, is a solid white gold dress watch dating to circa the 1970s. It was released just after the original Royal Oak Ref. 5402 and builds on the ultra-thin dress watch race that dominated this era. It even utilizes the very same movement that the Royal Oak did. It is constructed in such a way that the 'woven' bracelet completely encapsulates the mid-case. A true 'bracelet' dress watch. It measures 34mm in diameter at the widest point and like virtually any integrated-bracelet watch, it wears a bit larger than its 'on paper' dimensions would indicate. It also has a white gold crown at 3 o'clock, a screw-down caseback, and that ultra-thin automatic-winding calibre within. The dial is perfectly suited for this piece. Blue in color, it features a sunburst surface with applied diamond indices, a date aperture, and minimal text. It is beautifully-preserved and is tied together with a 'pencil' handset. When these first went on sale, they were positioned higher than not only the steel Royal Oak, but higher than the sold gold Royal Oaks. Compare their position on the market today, and it becomes clear that these remain a bargain despite their resurgence in popularity in the last few years. Stunning, rare, and objectively impressive, this piece is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be. Only in the last few years have collectors and enthusiasts alike started to pay a bit more attention to pieces like these and, we think, its long overdue.

title: Rolex Datejust Ref. 1600/3 - Blue 'Denim' Dial
description: Hard to believe - but the Datejust has been around since 1945. It is far older than its bigger and attention-hogging Submariner brethren. The Datejust was Rolex’s idea of the perfect everyday watch. The robustness of the Oyster case, combined with the elegance of an Oyster Perpetual. The ‘4 digit’ series of Datejust are particularly attractive for their pie-pan dials which offer a layer of three-dimensionality to the dials that went away with the advent of quickset date and 5-digit Datejusts. These early Datejusts were available as the 1601, with a fluted white gold bezel, or the 1603, with an engine-turned steel bezel. The 4-Digit Datejusts were also the first series to become available with a myriad of dial colors and case and bracelet materials. This particular piece is a very rare Reference 1600/3 dating to circa 1968. It comes to us in very nice overall condition, with a gently previously polished case and smooth yellow gold bezel, and a matching two-tone Jubilee bracelet. Sneaky rare reference aside, the dial within is the real highlight here. Blue in color, it features the same 'linen' texture that is most commonly found on silver and champagne colored dials, resulting in what can only be described as a 'denim' appearance. It remains in fantastic condition, with a nice vibrant blue color, fully-intact Tritium plots, and a nicely matching yellow gold handset. This is easily one of the rarest variants of a 4-digit Datejust that we have ever come across, and just like any vintage Datejust, it can easily be your one vintage watch or as an additional to a growing collection.

title: Patek Philippe Nautilus 'Jumbo' Ref. 3700/1AJ - Blue 'Teak' Dial
description: The Nautilus. Another Gerald Genta horological icon, sibling to the Royal Oak, and conductor of the Hype Train. Now that we have that out of the way, how did a brand like Patek Philippe get so famous for a steel time-only watch? Well, by accident. The Stern family, which still owns Patek, was constantly being asked back in the late 60s to make a steel sports watch. It turns out that loyal collectors of the brand who would buy their high complication watches and precious metal dress pieces had become so loyal to Patek - that they would only wear wristwatches from the illustrious brand. Not one to disappoint their well-heeled clientele, Gerald Genta was commissioned to design a sports watch worthy of the Patek name. Much like the Royal Oak, the steel case was treated to a wide variety of complex finishing techniques normally reserved for precious metals. While this was a sports piece, it was still to be a Patek Philippe above all else. Unlike the far more rugged Royal Oak, the Nautilus has gentler curves - and certainly no exposed bolts or rivets (can you imagine!). The piece that we have here is an example of the very first Nautilus — a Ref. 3700. And as you've probably noticed, this one is a solid yellow gold example. Like its stainless steel contemporaries, this is known as a 'Jumbo' for it's 40mm case diameter. And while that number may not seem so 'jumbo' by the standards of today, that was considerably larger than most watches in the 1970s — especially when you factor in the integrated bracelet and 'ears' on the case profiles which contribute to an even larger feel when on the wrist. Dating to the first few years of production, this Ref. 3700/1AJ is offered in exceptional overall condition. The case, bezel, and matching integrated bracelet show signs of having been professionally refurbished to factory specification and shows only faint wear. The bracelet remains tight and in matching condition. Inside, the characteristic blue 'teak' dial is exceptionally well-preserved. The surface is seemingly devoid of the 'flaking' or wear commonly found on colored dials from this era and has evenly patinated Tritium-filled applied indices and a matching yellow gold handset. Pretty neat if you ask us. As the saying goes: "You never actually own a Patek Philippe. You merely look after it for the next generation." This one is ready for it's next lucky caretaker.

title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 1803 - Sunburst Silver 'Swiss Only' Dial
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Lyndon B. Johnson was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a matching solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), but also on a leather strap like the example that we have here. The piece that we have here, a Reference 1803, dates to circa 1963, is a strong example finished in solid yellow gold with a silver 'Swiss Only' dial inside. The Oyster case remains thick and symmetrical and shows normal signs of wear throughout with a light 'rosy' tarnishing developing around the bezel and underside of the lugs. The characteristic 'fluted' yellow gold bezel also retains nice finishing with matching wear. The sunburst silver dial within retains a clear sunburst surface, with a light 'rosy' tarnishing visible on the 'door stop' indices, nicely patinated Tritium plots, and a matching 'obelisk' handset. It also happens to come fitted with a Rolex-signed brown leather strap with a signed yellow gold-tone buckle. Especially when fitted to a leather strap, this 'elevated' piece remains very much under-the-radar and is suitable for virtually any occasion, on virtually any wrist.

title: Cartier Lapis Lazuli Minute Repeater Clock - Silver dial w/ EWC Movement
description: By the mid 1970s, Cartier has secured itself as a global name in luxury goods — namely jewelry, and of course, watches. But prior to this time, the maison was much smaller and produced far fewer goods. As such, anything prior to the early 1970s can be considered special, rare, and usually interesting... And anything from earlier than the 1930s can be considered unobtanium ... So, when we came across this blue box from circa the 1920s, you might be able to imagine our reaction. You also may have noticed that this isn't even a watch. So whats going on? What we have here, of course, is a clock. But not just any clock... This piece is constructed out of brass and features cut slabs of the vibrant and alluring blue stone Lapis Lazuli which line all outer surfaces. Clearly, even in period, this would have been a high-end product, perhaps even a special order. The case envelops a simple silver dial that bears the Cartier and France script on the top half, an outer 'railroad' minute track, beautiful stylized-'Arabic' numerals rendered in Radium, and an equally stunning blued-steel 'cathedral' handset to match. The movement powering this piece is, as you'd expect from this era of Cartier, a European Watch & Clock Co. unit, operated by using the crown on the top. So what is the button on the right? Push it, wait a few seconds, and then you hear the chime of the minute and hours. Thats right, this clock is a minute repeater, and perhaps the coolest form of minute repeater in that it only appears to be a simple time-only clock. Now hopefully you can see what we couldn't resist... can you?

title: Rolex Precision 'Calatrava' Ref. 8896 - Satin Silver Dial
description: The 1950s was a decade that Rolex was really coming into their own. The 'Professional' line was almost immediately successful, giving the brand the capital to experiment and expand. The variety in metals, dials, and handsets in this era, particularly in the Oyster Perpetual, Oyster Precision, Datejust, and Day-Date families of watches was vast. It was also a time where the brand was playing around with manual-winding dress watches, usually denoted with 'Precision' on the dial. The piece that we have here comes from the 'Precision' family of watches and is about as close as you can get to a traditional, no frills 'Calatrava'-style dress watch from the brand. It features an attractive 34mm stainless steel case with a snapback design, a simple, unsigned crown, and attractive lugs running up to the 'stepped' topcase. Inside, the silver dial has a satin surface with minimal text, applied 'pencil' indices, and a patching 'dauphine' handset to match. And as we alluded to above, it is powered by a manual-winding movement. This then, is something of an exercise of restraint for Rolex. Their take on traditional, no frills Swiss watchmaking and an artifact of the brand before their direction largely changed towards the end of the twentieth century.

title: Movado Calendar 'Ladies' Ref. 13025 - 'Brushed' Silver Dial Unpolished
description: While it may be hard to imagine based upon their product line today, Movado Factories (yes, that was the full name) once made watches that were beautifully designed, exceptionally-well made, and respected on a level that matched the very best manufacturers. Some of their more sought-after models include the M90 and M95 chronographs of the 1940s - 1970s, the Sub-Sea range, and both time-only and complicated pieces that utilized case designs shared with brands like Patek Philippe, Mido, and DOXA. Those are all great models. We love them, and even collect them, but it allows for lesser-known pieces to slide through the cracks for most collectors... Take the watch that we have here for example: a ladies 'calendar' from the 1940s. It features a square 13mm x 13mm stainless steel case and remains in simply exceptional — very gently worn condition. The case utilizes a pair of micro-pushers on the left case profile for setting the day and date, as well as a crown at 3 o'clock for winding and setting the time. The dial has a lovely 'brushed' silver base with printed black 'exploding' indices on the outer edge, lovely silver 'foil' indices in the inside, and a a blue date track between the two. Time is read via a blued-steel 'dauphine' handset with a red 'pointer-date' hand. Last but not least, it is powered by one of Movado's own manual-winding movements. In our opinion, and we know there are a handful of other dealers and enthusiasts out there that share this viewpoint, there are not many brands that get design this right. Simple as that.

title: Tudor Ranger Date Ref. 7966/0 - Matte Black Dial w/ 'Roulette' Date Unpolished
description: The Tudor brand was born in 1926 out of a problem that Rolex founder Hans Wilsdorf had: It is much easier to produce high-quality Rolex Oyster cases at scale, than it is to produce the handmade, assembled, and tested Rolex movements that the cases bear. His brilliant solution, use ebauche calibres (off the shelf mass produced swiss movements from ETA, Valjoux, etc.) and pair them with the high-quality cases from Rolex. This would allow those cases to be used, and be able to offer a very high quality product at a much lower price-point. Many Tudor models even resembled and shared the names of their Rolex relatives: i.e. Submariner, Prince, Oyster, etc. The piece that we have here, an Prince Oysterdate 'Ranger' Ref. 7966/0, dates to circa 1968 and comes to us in strong overall condition. The 34mm Oyster case remains unpolished and retains thick, symmetrical lugs at all four corners and shows normal signs of wear. Like its Rolex cousin, the bezel is a smooth steel unit and is in matching condition. The real highlight with any Ranger, however, is the dial inside. Offered in both time-only variants or with a date, the remaining quadrant numerals are virtually identical to the beloved numerals found on Rolex's Explorer Ref. 1016. This example features the characteristic 6, 9, and 12 numerals at their respective locations, as well as a 'roulette' date at the 3 o'clock position. The indices themselves exhibit a light and uniform patina throughout with a correct, matching 'shovel'-style handset. It comes fitted to a period-correct Oyster bracelet with a signed blade clasp. This is a strong example of a vintage field watch that has seen steady grown in popularity, with no signs of stopping... ...and with the most recent modern interpretation of this piece being a hit, these vintage examples are being held and surface far less than they previously had on the open market.

title: CWC 'RAF' Chronograph Ref. 0552/924-3306 - Matte Black 'Gilt' Dial Unpolished
description: Cabot Watch Company, better known as CWC, was founded in 1972 by Ray Mellor, a former Royal Air Force serviceman who saw an opportunity as British military watch contracts began shifting away from long-established suppliers. Named after the explorer John Cabot, the company was established with a singular purpose: to produce robust, no-nonsense timepieces built to the exacting standards of the Ministry of Defence. Where earlier names like Smiths and Newmark had defined previous generations of British-made issued watches, CWC arrived at precisely the right moment to become the standard bearer for Britain's armed forces. For the next three decades, CWC supplied everything from General Service watches to chronographs and Royal Navy dive watches, earning a reputation through reliability rather than marketing. Its asymmetrical chronographs became a familiar sight on the wrists of military personnel, while the quartz-powered G10, introduced in the early 1980s, would go on to become one of the most widely issued British military watches ever produced. Although official procurement eventually broadened beyond CWC, the company never abandoned the military-first philosophy on which it was founded, and today its watches remain remarkably faithful to the original specifications that earned them their place in British service. The piece that we have here is chronograph issued to the Royal Air Force dating to circa 1975. It features a 39mm asymmetrical case, not dissimilar to that of what you'd find on a Speedmaster, complete with 'pump' pushers, a recessed crown, and a screw-down caseback. It has seemingly been spares of previous polishing, with nice defined finishing and shows normal wear throughout with clear military engravings on the caseback. Inside, the matte black dial features a very unusual 'gilt'-style of displaying the silver indices printing, with the exception of the 'CWC' text which is stamped. The Tritium indices have developed an attractive and uniform patina from age, and the correct white-painted 'sword' handset is a later set replaced under contract service. Powering this piece is a workhorse Valjoux Cal. 7733 manual-winding movement and it comes fitted to a very appropriate 'Admiralty Grey' NATO strap. Not only is this a piece of history, but when compared to other military-issued pieces from other brands, this actually is fantastic value, and they do not grow on trees!

title: Patek Philippe Ellipse 'TV' Ref. 3604-1J - Sunburst Blue 'Sigma' Dial
description: As far as brand identity goes, Patek Philippe, unlike many brands, is seemingly free of being associated with any one model in particular, and instead enjoys a reputation for quality, craftsmanship, and a long-standing pedigree as a top Swiss manufacturer. Of course, there are models and model families that are nothing short of icons (e.g., Nautilus, Calatrava, Grand Complications, etc.) but if you dig deep enough there are hidden gems that do not even fall into any of these families. The Ellipse family of watches, for example, was all but forgotten — or just overlooked — for decades until the last 4-5 years. When they were sold new, these were regarded as extremely high-end and opulent timepieces and have remained relative bargains next to, lets say, their more sport-oriented steel siblings. The piece that we have here is amongst the most sought-after Ellipse models, with a large 36mm x 36mm solid yellow gold 'TV' case, an integrated 'woven' yellow gold bracelet, and a sunburst blue dial within. It remains in strong overall condition, with visible hallmarks, a correct signed crown, and shows normal signs of wear from age. The dial inside is almost entirely devoid of the usual wear or degradation found on colored dials from this era and presents beautifully. It features applied 'pencil' indices, a framed date aperture, and a matching 'dauphine' handset. No doubt, however, the highlight of this piece is that stunning 'woven' bracelet constructed out of solid yellow gold. It shows matching normal wear to that of the case and utilized a familiar signed locking clasp commonly found during this era. Calatrava or complications aren't for you? Look no further.

title: Longines 'Hooded Lug' Rectangular Dress Watch - Silver 'Art Deco' Dial LNOS w/ Tags
description: Longines is one of the most well respected manufacturers of the 20th century, full stop. Founded in 1832 in Saint-Imier, Switzerland, the company built a name for themselves early on as a manufacturer of quality in-house movements right from the start. Throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Longines also built a reputation for precision timekeeping, earning accolades at international exhibitions and becoming a trusted name in sports timing, particularly in horse racing and aviation — an association with continues until today. By the mid-20th century, especially from the 1930s to the 1960s, Longines was at the peak of its technical and aesthetic prowess, producing a range of high-grade wristwatches admired today by collectors and vintage enthusiasts. The brand was known for its beautifully finished in-house movements, such as the 13ZN and 30CH chronographs, which are considered some of the finest column-wheel chronographs ever produced. The piece that we have here is an incredibly attractive 'Art Deco' rectangular dress watch dating to circa 1937 and simply put, it is offered in virtually new-old-stock condition. The case measures in at 22mm x 34.5mm — roughly the same size as the Reverso from JLC from this era — with fantastic 'hooded' lugs, and a flat crown. Inside, the silver dial is even more reminiscent of a Reverso, with a silver multi-tone silver color-way, stunning silver 'foil' indices, blakc 'Arabic' numerals, and a blued-steel 'feuille' handset. It even comes with a pair of hangtags! As it pertains to vintage collecting, this checks a heck of a lot of boxes; A niche brand with historically important innovations, fantastic sizing, and virtually flawless condition. What more can you ask for?

title: Rolex GMT-Master Ref. 1675 'PCG' - Gilt 'Chapter Ring' Dial
description: The Rolex GMT-Master is one of the most historic and iconic watches the brand ever produced. Its origin dates back to a commission request by Pan American World Airways in the early 50’s for their fleet of pilots who needed access to different time zones. These pieces would feature a similar design to another watch that Rolex was developing around that time, the Submariner, but would include a fourth hand running on 24-hr time, and a bi-colored bezel insert to represent AM/PM times. Those colors, naturally, would be the PanAm colors: Red & Blue. Thus, in 1953, the Ref. 6542 GMT-Master was born. These early pieces were ultimately, fragile arguably flawed in some ways, and were therefor succeeded by the updated Reference 1675 in 1959. These pieces introduced a larger case size with crown-guards and a bi-colored blue + red bezel insert made of aluminum. The Ref. 1675 underwent many small changes over its 21-year production run, with a slew of dial, bezel, bracelet, and hand variations. You know, Rolex stuff. The example that we have here dates to circa 1961 and is an uncommon variant from within the 1675 range, featuring not only a 'gilt' dial, but also a case with 'pointed' crown guards. For a very short time, the 1675 case features more pronounced and stylized crown guards along with the gorgeous wide lug chamfers that we all know and love. The case has been lightly polished at an earlier time, thankfully done so tastefully where the lugs remain thick and symmetrical with, while faint, visible factory chamfers. Crucially, the characteristic 'pointed' crown guards are clear and defined. Inside, the dial presents beautifully, with a largely clean glossy black surface and gorgeous, patinated luminous plots. The handset matches the dial beautifully and has the correct 'small' 24-hr GMT hand. It comes fitted to a correct 'rivet' Oyster bracelet with a blade clasp. And then, of course, there is that gorgeous 'Pepsi' bezel insert. It shows only light wear throughout and retains a rich blue and red colors. All of these small details amount to a piece that not only has a wearing experience different than any modern GMT-Master, but even later variants of the very same Reference. Its fair to say that watches from this era, in this overall condition do not surface all that often...

title: CYMA 'Clamshell' Chronograph - Black Gilt 'Multi-Scale' Non-Luminous Dial Unpolished
description: CYMA’s rise to prominence was shaped by one of the most successful partnerships in early Swiss watchmaking. Founded by the Schwob brothers, the company had already established itself as a highly capable manufacturer, recognized for efficiently assembling quality watches from Swiss-made components. A pivotal moment came in 1891 when Henri Sandoz, founder of Tavannes Watch Company, relocated his operations from Le Locle to the village of Tavannes. Sandoz brought with him considerable expertise in complicated watchmaking—particularly repeaters and chronographs—complementing CYMA’s industrial organization and manufacturing strength. What began as a practical collaboration quickly proved mutually advantageous, leading to a formal merger in 1903. In the years that followed, the combined enterprise operated under the names CYMA, Tavannes, and CYMA-Tavannes, reflecting a shared commitment to precision, innovation, and manufacturing excellence. By 1910, the company had become one of Switzerland’s largest watch producers, distinguished by its advanced standardization of parts and remarkably consistent production quality. While Sandoz’s influence reinforced the firm's reputation for sophisticated chronographs, it was the combined technical expertise of both companies that established CYMA and Tavannes as one of the most capable and forward-thinking forces in Swiss watchmaking during the early twentieth century. The piece that we have here is perhaps the crème de la crème in the world of vintage CYMA: a 'jumbo-clamshell' chronograph with a 'gilt-multi-scale' dial. Coming in at 38mm in diameter with a 20mm lug spacing and oversize 'pump' pushers, this piece has presence on the wrist even today. It remains in unpolished condition, with nice symmetrical downturned lugs and nice finishing present throughout. The dial inside is very nicely preserved — no doubt due in part to its lack of luminous material degrading over its eighty-years of life — retaining excellent printing throughout with a gentle patina across the surface and a matching gold-tone 'feuille' handset. Last but not least, this piece is powered by the legendary Valjoux 22 manual-winding movement. You don't just land on CYMA. This, along with brands like Movado, Universal Genève, etc. are found years into collection and exploration of this hobby. And on top of being elusive, strong examples are more elusive still, as collectors tend to hang onto good ones. This is a good one. *This piece comes from the personal collection of our founder*

title: Rolex Two-Tone Rectangular Dress Watch Ref. 1378 - Sunburst Silver Dial
description: Prior to becoming perhaps the most powerful, well-known watch brand on the planet, Rolex was just like any other small manufacturer in the first half of the twentieth century. Before major model families came into their own, such as the Datejust, Day-Date, and the entirety of the Professional range, they were constantly experimenting trying new things to see what stuck. The Prince family of watches, while niche, are known to collectors and enthusiasts and offer a rich variety of metals, dials, and design from the early twentieth century. The piece that we have here, a two-tone rectangular dress watch, is another rectangular model that has somehow alluded collector circles, and what a beauty it is. It features a 21mm x 35mm 9k yellow gold outer case with fixed 'wire' lugs, and a stainless steel inner case that houses the movement and dial. The 9k winding crown is recessed and very likely original to the watch. The silver dial inside is very nicely preserved, with a nice vibrant sunburst surface with very simple printed indices and a blued-steel handset. Dating to circa the early 1950s, this represents the very end of the Art-Deco era for Rolex and seems to be completely overlooked, or flat-out forgotten. The upside is that they present fantastic value relative to the usual suspects from the brand, and you're very, very unlikely to see another in the wild.

title: Breitling Chronorgaph 'Mid Size' - Gloss Black 'Multi-Scale' Dial Unpolished
description: Breitling has a long and rich history in chronographs — with an emphasis on aviation chronographs. And like so many other brands who have a watch model, or family that has become synonymous with the brand name itself, the Navitimer is just that for Breitling. As a result, the Navitimer casts a substantial shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the SuperOcean, Top Time, and lesser-known pieces that pre-date model ranges all together. The example that we have here is one of the latter: A chronograph dating to circa the 1940s. Offered in phenomenal overall condition, this piece possesses many of the hallmark design characteristics found in many vintage Breitling chronographs. The case measures in at 32mm in diameter and features fantastic and attractive lugs, 'square' pushers, a snapback caseback, and a high-polished 'stepped' bezel. It shows light signs of wear with nice, defined finishing present throughout. The crown shows some 'brassing' from use and operates the Venus calibre within. The dial is wonderfully preserved, with a rich glossy black surface, clear scales and printing, and a 'stacked' register layout. The luminous indices exhibit a light and largely uniform patina and are complimented by a correct 'kite' handset. Vintage chronographs in condition like this, from any brand, are surprisingly elusive. Collectors tend to hold onto fantastic examples like this one, and with its slightly smaller size, this one presents fantastic value relative to larger contemporaries in comparable condition. *This piece comes from the personal collection of our founder*

title: Universal Genève Space-Compax Ref. 885104/01 - 'Mk1' Reverse-Panda Dial
description: Universal Genève was one of the many great brands that succumbed to the quartz crisis of the 1970s. While they disappeared, it was not for their lack of impressive watches. To underscore that fact, keep in mind that Henri Stern Watch Agency in their nearly 80-year history has only ever sold two brands: Patek Philippe, and Universal Genève. Building upon the brand’s long-established Compax lineage, the Space-Compax was i ntroduced during the 1960s at the height of the Space Age and represented Universal Genève’s answer to the growing demand for technically sophisticated, modern chronographs. And the Space-Compax sure delivered, combining a highly legible three-register chronograph layout with a distinctive design language with a technically forward-thinking form. The asymmetrical case measures in at 40mm in diameter and utilized a screw-down caseback, screw-down crown, and even a water-resistant pusher design. Rather than simple 'pump' pushers, the mechanisms are capped with rubber and secured by a screw-down 'collar,' effectively providing a sealed pusher. The bezel is a single piece rather than an assembly with an insert, and doubles-down on the timing functionality with 60-minute marks and a colored market at the 12 o'clock position. Inside, the dial is characterized by bold indices, contrasting 'concentric' subsidiary registers, and colorful accents with a both colorful and bold handset tying it all together. These pieces were all powered by UG's Cal. 85 manual-winding movement. The example that we have here, a Ref. 885104/02, dates to circa 1967 and is offered in fantastic overall condition. The case shows signs of very light previous polished, perhaps on the case profiles only, with normal signs of wear and no damage or excess wear of note. The pushers, crown, and bezel all show light wear and present beautifully. The dial within, likely due to its resistance to the elements, is also wonderfully preserved, with a nice clean surface, crisp subsidiary registers, and fully-intact luminous elements. Additionally, it comes fitted to its correct and exceedingly rare, 'double-grain beads-of-rice' Gay Frères bracelet with the correct endlinks and signed fliplock clasp. Design details like the dynamic and modern sizing of the case, the calibre within, and the thoughtful, bold dial layout, amount to a piece that clearly shows why Universal Genève was ultimately considered to be one of the finest manufactures in the era. In any condition, Space-Compaxes simply do not surface on the open market all that often — let alone in this condition and with its correct bracelet.... and with the recent re-launch of the brand, collectors seem to be holding on to pieces like this, making for a great opportunity to grab this one.

title: Rolex Day-Date Ref. 1803 - Sunburst Champagne 'Wide Boy-Sigma' Dial Unpolished W/ Box & Papers
description: When the Day-Date was released in 1956, Rolex had made numerous attempts to capture the market with more complicated timepieces such as the Ref. 6036, the Ref. 8171, and the Ref. 6062, but it seemed like buyers were not particularly fond of complicated Rolexes. All of that changed when President Lyndon B. Johnson was spotted wearing one Rolex in particular: a Day-Date. The model has since become known worldwide as ‘The President’ and as a symbol of success and prestige. Simply put, this one stuck. The Day-Date was available for many years on a leather strap with a matching gold buckle, but also on a solid gold bracelet (called a 'President' bracelet), like the example that we have here. The piece that we have here, a Reference 1803, dates to circa 1971, is a strong example finished in solid yellow gold with a classic champagne dial. The Oyster case remains thick and symmetrical, seemingly unpolished and shows normal signs of wear throughout with clear hallmarks on the lug undersides. The characteristic 'fluted' yellow gold bezel also retains nice definition with matching wear. The sunburst champagne dial within is exceptional. As vibrant as ever, it features excellent, evenly patinated Tritium plots, applied 'wide boy' indices, and a matching handset. Especially when fitted to a leather strap, this 'elevated' piece remains very much under-the-radar and is suitable for virtually any occasion, on virtually any wrist.

title: Rolex Oyster Perpetual Date Ref. 1501 - Black 'Gilt' Dial
description: If you boil Rolex down to its purest form, what do you get? The Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is truly the genesis for the entire Rolex brand. The very first Rolex models were called ‘Oysters’ which was owed to their innovative three part case that all screwed into each-other. That is where the fluted bezel actually derives from, being screwed down into the top of the case to secure the crystal with a gasket - as well as the grooves on the oyster case back. All makes sense now - right? The piece that we have here, simply known as an Oyster Perpetual Date , is a descendant of those early watches, utilizing a water-resistant Oyster case, an automatic-winding movement, and a date complication. A functional, sturdy, and dependable timekeeping device. Dating to circa 1965, this Reference 1501 features a 34mm Oyster case with a period-correct 'rivet' Oyster bracelet with blade clasp, and a unique to this reference, 'engine-turned' steel bezel. The case, bezel and bracelet have all seemingly been spared of any previous polishing and show normal wear from age and use. Inside, dial is nicely preserved and retains its rich glossy black surface with that gorgeous gilt text, applied indices, and a matching handset. The Oyster Perpetual line presents great value next to its slightly larger Datejust siblings, while simultaneously representing the essence of Rolex. This example, with its rich, versatile dial, is not just a great entry point to a vintage Rolex, but could easily be your one vintage watch.

title: Rolex Oyster Precision Ref. 6512 'Veriflat' - Sunburst Silver 'Asprey' Dial

The handset matches the dial beautifully and has the correct 'small' 24-hr GMT hand. And then, of course, there is that gorgeous 'Pepsi' bezel insert. It shows only normal wear from age and has developed an attractive fade on both the blue and red halves. Last but not least, this piece is accompanied by its box, chronometer papers, and guarantee papers dated 9/24/1962. All of these small details amount to a piece that not only has a wearing experience different than any modern GMT-Master, but even later variants of the very same Reference. Its fair to say that watches from this era, in this overall condition do not surface all that often...

title: Audemars Piguet White Gold Dress Watch - White Gold 'Woven' Dial w/ 'Sodalite' Indices
description: The year 1972 was the advent of what is undeniably Audemars Piguet's most famous, significant, and yes, iconic line of watches, the Royal Oak. It was also the year that the 'high-end dress watch' would forever change. Prior to 1972, ultra-thin and design-focused precious metal watches represented the pinnacle of the genre, not what appears to be an industrial-styled stainless steel sports watch with a bracelet. While the brand never stopped producing traditional dress watches, per-se, production of their new golden goose would dominate the rest of the lineup. And this is after considering that prior to the Royal Oak, AP made far fewer watches to start with... The piece that we have here hails from circa the 1980s, an era when brands like Patek Philippe, Audemars Piguet, Piaget, and even Rolex were experimenting with design-forward timepieces focused on finishing and opulence. The 26mm case and matching integrated-style bracelet are constructed out of solid white gold, with a stunning hand-finished texture throughout. The dial inside is not flat, but rather a 3-dimensional 'woven' white gold base with applied 'Soladite' stone indices, and thats it. A clean design that speaks by way of its execution rather than text. The blue stone indices are complimented by a blue-painted 'pencil' handset. It is powered by AP's Cal. 2003 manual-winding movement. Stunning, rare, and objectively impressive. This then, is a representation of a bygone era not just for Audemars Piguet, but for what a high-end dress watch used to be. Only in the last few years have collectors and enthusiasts alike started to pay a bit more attention to pieces like these and, we think, its long overdue.

title: Eberhard and Co. Contograf Ref. 131501 - Sunburst Silver Non-Luminous Dial Unpolished
description: The Eberhard Contograf is one of the best looking and most interesting chronographs of the 20th century and when Eberhard introduced the Contograf in the 1960s, it was like nothing else on the market. Eberhard always tried to think outside the box and be innovative, hence the unusual date placement at six o’clock (still uncommon even today) and date corrector at nine o’clock. The Contograf is largely black with a few red details in the alternating red numbers on the ‘roulette’ date wheel, the red triangle at the 12 o’clock on the bezel, and the 50 at the two o’clock position on the dial. That red “50” in the tachymeter scale marks 50 km/hr, which at the time was the standard speed limit in most European countries. These details cater to the overall sportiness of the Contograf, and when combined with always attractive features like a twin-register dial, virtually perfect case proportions, and a manual-winding calibre, amount to a watch with loads of character in a subtle fashion. The example that we have here comes from the latter half of the Contograf's run and, while all Contografs are rare, this variant is rarer still. Dating to the late 1960s, it features an outstanding unpolished case with prominent chamfers, a correct signed crown, 'pump' pushers, and a screw-down caseback. It shows normal wear throughout with no damage or wear of note. The bezel insert also remains in strong overall condition, showing normal wear with a clear red accent in the triangle. The real highlight here, is the silver dial within. Produced in even fewer numbers than the usual black-dial piece, this silver dial features a crisp and vibrant sunburst finishing throughout and happens to be in exceptionally well-preserved condition. Like its black-dial contemporaries, it has applied indices, a framed date aperture at the 6 o'clock position, those amazing red accents, and one of the coolest script logos ever to grace a watch dial. And best of all, it is a Contograf. A watch that we like to think as something of a Submariner-Speedmaster hybrid. Seldom seen to begin with, we feel that this is one of the coolest vintage watches of all time, full stop. This example takes what is already a masterwork in design to another level with it's fantastic overall condition and elegant silver dial.

title: Omega 'Calatrava' Cal. 26.5.T3 - Gloss Black 'Gilt' Dial
description: Omega is undeniably one of the most historically important timepiece manufactures of all time. In fact, the Speedmaster is probably the most important wrist watch of all time. As a result, the Speedmaster casts a massive shadow over all of its siblings.... even over firmly planted models like the Seamaster and Constellation ranges. The resulting effect is double sided: many vintage Omegas, we feel are incredibly undervalued in the market as it exists today, with the other side of that being that hidden gems are shocking attainable. Take the piece that we haver here, a stainless steel Calatrava-style time-only watch dating to circa 1943. This Ref. 2383-6 has a ton going for it. The 30mm case is wonderfully preserved and in excellent condition, with crisp lug holes and symmetrical proportions. It also features a steel crown at 3 o'clock, a screw-down caseback, and Omega's own Cal. 26.5.T3 manual-winding movement inside. The dial however, is the highlight of this particular example. Like the case, it is wonderfully preserved, with a rich glossy black surface that shows only faint signs of aging with stunning patinated Radium 'Roman' indices. It is complimented by a 'sword' handset that matches nicely. This piece, with its sizing, condition, and completely unique dial really embodies everything that makes vintage great. What more can you ask for?

title: Tudor Submariner Date Ref. 79090 - Blue Dial Unpolished
description: The Submariner, namely those produced by Rolex, has long been considered the cream of the crop when it comes to watch collecting as a whole. Possibly the most iconic watch ever produced, the Submariner has long standing utilitarian roots that span decades, and everyone who’s anyone has been spotted wearing one. However, if you look deeper into the Submariner line, you may find a less known but just as incredible model manufactured by Tudor. These pieces are not only more unique and rare than the traditional Submariner, but offer much greater value. Designed as a replacement for the quintessential Tudor ‘Snowflake’ Submariners, the References 76100 and 79090 is in many collectors eyes, the last great vintage Tudor Submariner. These pieces all had matte dials with Tritium plots and matching Tritium-filled handsets, cases with lug-holes, acrylic crystals, and folded-link Oyster bracelets. In many ways, This is all stuff that we see in Rolex and Tudor models as early as the 1960s, but were produced well-into the 1990s! The example that we have here dates to circa 1988 and remains in outstanding overall condition. The case remains unpolished, with clear factory finishing visible throughout and shows normal wear from age. The bezel also remains unpolished, with excellent definition and houses a gorgeous blue insert with a patinated pip. Inside, it features a desirable blue dial, which retains a rich, deep blue color and attractive patinated Tritium indices and a matching handset. It comes fitted to its correct steel Oyster bracelet with a Tudor-signed fliplock clasp. These Tudor Subs of the mid 1980s into the mid 1990s not only present great value next to their Rolex cousins, but are very interesting in that they offer nearly all the feel of a Rolex Submariner Date dating back to the 1960s — with the charm of an acrylic crystal, a matte dial, and even a folded-link bracelet — for only a fraction of the entry cost. And Rolex sure never made a steel Submariner with a blue dial!

title: Tudor Black Bay Fifty-Eight Ref. 79030N - 'Rowing Blazers' Box & Booklets
description: Our roots and indeed our passion for watches are firmly planted in the world of vintage — of course. And while there are modern collections that capture that vintage soul and aesthetic, there are few as well executed as Tudor's Black Bay family. Introduced in 2012 along with the Pelagos line, the Black Bay aimed to tribute divers from both Tudor and Rolex from the late 1950s-1960s, and to say that it was an immediate success would be a drastic understatement. What began as a simple black-dial, stainless steel model has since evolved into a more adventurous lineup, now offered in a wide variety of sizes, dial colors, and even materials like bronze, solid gold, and sterling silver. It has no doubt become Tudors most known family of watches, particularly the 39mm 'Fifty-Eight.' Released a few years after the original 'Heritage' Black Bay, the 'BB58' drew nearly everything from the original Black Bays 41mm size, are repackaged it in a more sleek, remarkably wearable size and with an updated movement. The example that we have here, a Ref. 79030N, is probably exactly what comes to mind when you hear "Black Bay." However, look a little closer and you'll note the additional white text on the dial that reads: "Rowing Blazers." In 2023, Rowing Blazers offered less than 100 of very special Black Bay Fifty-Eights exclusively to 'Friends & Family' of the brand. This is one of those watches. Like any other steel BB58, it features a 39mm case with beautiful lug chamfers, a Tudor 'rose' signed screw-down crown with no crown guards in sight, a METAS-certified automatic-winding movement, a beautiful satin black 'gilt'-like dial with applied luminous plots and a 'Snowflake' handset, and a 'rivet'-style Oyster bracelet with a fliplock clasp. Offered in gently worn condition with many of its factory stickers in place, it comes accompanied by its inner and outer boxes and booklets.

title: Rolex Oyster Perpetual Ref. 6548 'Midsize' - Sunburst Silver 'Linz' Dial
description: If you boil Rolex down to its purest form, what do you get? The Rolex Oyster Perpetual. This is truly the genesis for the entire Rolex brand. The very first Rolex models were called ‘Oysters’ which was owed to their innovative three part case that all screwed into each-other. That is where the fluted bezel actually derives from, being screwed down into the top of the case to secure the crystal with a gasket - as well as the grooves on the oyster case back. All makes sense now - right? The piece that we have here is a descendant of those early watches, though probably not what you first think of when you hear Oyster Perpetual ... This is a 'midsize' Oyster Perpetual Ref. 6548 dating to circa 1962. It comes in at 30mm in diameter and is constructed out of 14k yellow gold and it remains in strong overall condition. The case and matching 'smooth' yellow gold bezel have been gently previously polished many years ago and shows light signs of wear throughout with an attractive 'rosy' oxidation developing in some areas. Inside, the silver dial features a crisp sunburst finishing on the surface, with applied stylized-indices, patinated Tritium pots, and a matching 'dauphine' handset. Look a little closer and you'll find an additional retailer stamp on the lower half of the dial from Dallas' Linz. Despite being ‘entry-level,' many vintage models from the Oyster family offer a ton of character and remain an overlooked part of the important history of Rolex on their journey to the powerhouse brand that they are today. And don't let the case size fool you, 30mm can accommodate a wider range of wrists than most think. This one, with is 14k construction, special dial, and overall condition stands out from not just its OP siblings, but punches way above its class.

title: Movado M95 Chronograph Ref. 19038 - 'Sub Sea' Satin Silver Dial
description: While it may be hard to imagine based upon their product line today, Movado Factories (yes, that was the full name) once made watches that were beautifully designed, exceptionally-well made, and respected on a level that matched the very best manufacturers. The piece that we have here, an M95 Chronograph, is simply named after the Movado Manufacture M95 movement powering it. Over the years, these were produced with a variety of dial and case configurations, with this example having been produced on the later end dating to circa the early 1960s. The 35mm 'waterproof' case shares a similar design and in fact, the same case-maker as properly heavy hitting references from this era. That is, of course, François Borgel. It features gorgeous 'stepped' finishing on the top case, with dynamic, faceted lugs, a screw-down caseback, 'pump' pushers, and a 'domed' crown. The condition of this example is excellent, with strong factory finishing present throughout and the correct crown and pushers. Inside, the dial is one of the more 'sporty' variants, with a satin silver color throughout, applied Tritium-filled 'dart' indices, and a matching handset with red chronograph hands. Additionally, a very thoughtful and almost funny detail often found on Movado chronographs is how Movado chose to actually apply 'cropped' numerals around subsidiary registers where appropriate, in this case, at the 3, 6, & 9 o'clock positions. This detail is a great example of Movado exercising their prowess in design and manufacturing during this time and is an incredibly thoughtful detail that they easily could have skipped and nobody would have thought twice about it. Of course, this piece is powered by Movado's fantastic in-house Calibre M95 manually-wound movement. Both M95s and M90s have become extremely coveted by collectors and don't come to market as often as you may think... This piece, in its well-rounded and honest overall condition, is yet another example of the amazing value that Movado from this era offers. In our opinion, and we know there are a handful of other dealers and enthusiasts out there that share this viewpoint, there are not many brands that get design this right. Simple as that.

title: Audemars Piguet White Gold 'Ellipse' Dress Watch - Grey Dial w/ 'Lapis Lazuli' Indices
